scenarios.title: The loop that modifies copies
scenarios.situation: A normalization pass iterates a vector of readings with a range-for loop, but the values in the vector never change.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the mutation not stick?
evidence: for (auto r : readings) { r = (r - min) / (max - min); }  // vector unchanged
choices: auto deduces a by-value copy — each iteration mutates a temporary; use auto& to bind the actual element
Range-for loops are const by default — add the mutable keyword
auto cannot deduce numeric types in loops — write double r explicitly
The assignment needs std::move — r = std::move(...) instead
scenarios.why: In for (auto r : readings), r is a fresh copy of each element; writes to r die with the iteration. for (auto& r : readings) binds a reference to the element itself, so mutations persist. Use const auto& when only reading, to avoid copies of expensive types.
scenarios.hint: Is r the element, or a copy of the element?

scenarios.title: The object that is a function
scenarios.situation: A developer writes Widget w(); expecting a default-constructed Widget, then gets bizarre errors when calling w.reset().
scenarios.prompt: What did the declaration actually declare?
evidence:
Widget w();   // not an object!
w.reset();  // error: request for member in non-class type
choices: The most vexing parse: w is declared as a function taking no arguments and returning Widget — use Widget w{} or Widget w;
Parentheses are required for construction — the compiler needs a flag to accept it
Widget has no default constructor — this declares an abstract placeholder
w is a function pointer — call it as w()->reset()
scenarios.why: C++ grammar prefers to parse Widget w(); as a function declaration (returning Widget, taking no parameters) rather than a variable definition. Brace initialization Widget w{} unambiguously defines an object — and additionally forbids narrowing conversions.
scenarios.hint: When a statement can be parsed as either a declaration or a definition, which does the grammar prefer?

scenarios.title: The initializer that refuses to compile
scenarios.situation: A config struct initialized with braces fails to compile when a double is passed for an int field, while the parenthesized version compiled silently.
scenarios.prompt: What protection does brace initialization provide?
choices: Braced initialization forbids narrowing conversions — the error caught a lossy double-to-int conversion that parentheses would silently allow
Braces zero-initialize — l1.max_conn is 0, not 100
Uniform initialization only works for aggregates — Limits needs a constructor
The error is a compiler bug — both forms must behave identically
scenarios.why: List initialization (braces) makes narrowing conversions — those that can lose information, like double→int — ill-formed. Parenthesized and = initialization permit them silently. Preferring braces turns accidental truncation into a compile-time error at the point of the mistake.
scenarios.hint: Which initialization form did the standards committee make reject lossy conversions?

scenarios.title: The getter that will not compile on const objects
scenarios.situation: A getter works on regular objects but fails to compile when called through a const reference, breaking a read-only API.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the const context reject the call?
choices: count() is not marked const, so it cannot be called on a const object — add const after the parameter list
const references cannot call any member functions — take Store by value
std::cout is not const-correct — the error is in the stream, not the getter
Getters must be static — make count() a static member
scenarios.why: A member function without the trailing const is treated as potentially mutating, so the type system forbids calling it on const objects. Marking it int count() const promises read-only access and makes it callable in const contexts. Const-correctness is viral: one non-const getter poisons every const caller.
scenarios.hint: What does the compiler assume a member function might do unless you promise otherwise?

scenarios.title: The header that pollutes everything
scenarios.situation: A widely included header has using namespace std; at the top. Unrelated .cpp files start failing with ambiguous symbol errors after an unrelated library upgrade.
scenarios.prompt: Why is using namespace in headers dangerous?
evidence:
using namespace std;  // in a header: affects every includer
// ... later, someone's `count` collides with std::count
choices: The directive dumps every std name into the global namespace of every translation unit that includes the header — use explicit std:: qualification or targeted using-declarations in headers
Headers cannot contain using directives — it is a compile error being suppressed
std:: names are macros — they expand differently per translation unit
The upgrade renamed std::count — pin the library version instead
scenarios.why: A using-directive in a header is transitive: everyone who includes it (directly or indirectly) gets the entire namespace injected, inviting collisions like a local count vs std::count and silently changing overload resolution. Keep using-directives in .cpp files after all includes, or qualify with std::.
scenarios.hint: Who else is affected by a using-directive at the top of a header — just that header, or everyone who includes it?

scenarios.title: The surprising overload
scenarios.situation: Calling log(0) with overloads for log(long) and log(const std::string&) compiles but picks an unexpected overload after a refactor changed int overloads.
scenarios.prompt: How does overload resolution rank the candidates?
choices: Overload resolution prefers standard conversions (int→long) over user-defined conversions (int→std::string via constructor) — the ranking is exact match, promotion, conversion, user-defined
The first declared overload always wins ties — reorder the declarations
0 is a null pointer constant — it always selects pointer overloads
Overloads are resolved at link time — the linker picked arbitrarily
scenarios.why: Overload resolution ranks implicit conversion sequences: exact match first, then integral/floating promotions, then other standard conversions (int→long), and only then user-defined conversions (via a converting constructor to std::string). Understanding the ranking predicts which overload is chosen without trial and error.
scenarios.hint: Which requires more work from the compiler: converting int to long, or constructing a std::string from an int?

scenarios.title: The Dangling Else of Integer Division
scenarios.situation: A junior's telemetry function computes `double ratio = packets / total;` where both are `int`. With packets=3, total=4, the dashboard shows 0.0 instead of 0.75. The junior 'fixes' it by changing the return type to double, which changes nothing.
scenarios.prompt: What is the real bug and the minimal correct fix?
choices: The function signature is wrong; make the parameters double
Integer division happens before the assignment: cast one operand — `double ratio = static_cast<double>(packets) / total;`
The compiler optimizes the division away; disable -O2
Use float instead of double for the ratio variable
scenarios.why: In C++, `packets / total` with two ints performs integer division (result 0) and only then converts to double — the cast must happen on an operand, not the result. Changing the variable type (or float vs double) doesn't touch the division itself. This is the classic exam/interview trap: the conversion happens too late.
scenarios.hint: When does the int-to-double conversion happen relative to the division?
evidence: Places cast on operand, not result

scenarios.title: const Correctness Breaks the Build
scenarios.situation: You're adding a `getName()` accessor to a class. The codebase calls it on const objects in several places, and the build fails with 'discards qualifiers'. A teammate suggests removing const from the calling objects to 'make it compile'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct fix?
choices: Remove const from the calling objects as suggested
Mark the accessor const: `std::string getName() const;` — the method promises not to mutate, so it works on const objects
Make getName() a static method
const_cast away constness inside the accessor
scenarios.why: A non-const member function cannot be called on a const object — the fix is declaring the accessor const, which is a compile-time promise of non-mutation. Stripping const from callers (A) weakens the whole codebase's guarantees; static (C) loses access to members; const_cast (D) lies to the compiler and risks UB on genuinely-const objects.
scenarios.hint: The method's contract should say 'I won't modify anything' — where does that promise go?

scenarios.title: The derived destructor that never runs
scenarios.situation: Objects are deleted through a base-class pointer. Derived destructors never execute and resources leak, though the code compiles cleanly.
scenarios.prompt: What is missing from the base class?
choices: The base destructor must be virtual — without it, deleting through a base pointer is undefined behavior and skips derived cleanup
Derived needs to redeclare the destructor as override — the base one is fine
Delete must be called on the derived pointer type — store Derived* instead
Destructors cannot be virtual — use a virtual close() method and call it manually
scenarios.why: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer without a virtual destructor is undefined behavior; in practice the derived destructor (and member destruction) is skipped, leaking resources. Rule: any class designed as a base with polymorphic use needs a virtual destructor — often virtual ~Base() = default.
scenarios.hint: When delete runs through a Base*, how does it know which destructor code to execute?

scenarios.title: The derived part that got sliced off
scenarios.situation: A function takes a Base by value and is passed Derived objects. Virtual calls inside behave like the base, and derived data is gone.
scenarios.prompt: What happened to the derived portion?
evidence:
void process(Base b) { b.speak(); }  // takes Base BY VALUE
Derived d; process(d);  // d sliced to its Base subobject; speak() is Base's
choices: Object slicing: copying a Derived into a Base copies only the Base subobject — pass by reference (const Base&) to preserve polymorphism
Virtual dispatch requires pointers — references do not dispatch virtually
The copy constructor is implicitly deleted — the code should not compile
Derived's vtable pointer is null after the copy — initialize it manually
scenarios.why: Copying a derived object into a base-typed variable slices off everything beyond the base subobject, including the dynamic type — virtual calls then resolve to Base. Passing by (const) reference or pointer keeps the complete object and its dynamic type intact. Slicing is silent and compiles without warnings.
scenarios.hint: What fits in a Base-sized variable when you hand it a bigger Derived object?

scenarios.title: The override that was not
scenarios.situation: A derived class intends to override a base virtual function, but the base version keeps getting called. No compiler error appears.
scenarios.prompt: Why did the override silently fail, and which keyword prevents this?
choices: draw(long) has a different signature, so it hides rather than overrides — marking it override makes the mismatch a compile error
Virtual functions cannot be redeclared in derived classes — remove the declaration
int and long are the same type on this platform — the bug is elsewhere
The base pointer must be cast to Derived* for virtual dispatch
scenarios.why: Overriding requires an identical signature (plus compatible return types). draw(long) is a different function that hides the base name instead of overriding it. The override specifier makes the compiler verify the override — a signature mismatch becomes an error at the declaration, not a silent runtime surprise.
scenarios.hint: For a derived function to override, what must match exactly — and what helps the compiler check that for you?

scenarios.title: The virtual call in the constructor
scenarios.situation: A base constructor calls a virtual setup() method expecting the derived version, but the base version runs instead.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the virtual call not dispatch to the derived class during construction?
choices: During base construction the object's dynamic type is Base — the derived part does not exist yet, so virtual calls resolve to the base version
Constructors cannot call member functions — move the call after construction
setup() must be pure virtual for dispatch to work in constructors
The vtable is null until construction completes — virtual calls crash, not fall back
scenarios.why: While the base constructor runs, the derived members have not been constructed — the object's dynamic type is effectively the base. Virtual dispatch therefore resolves within the base. Calling a pure virtual from a constructor is even worse (undefined behavior). The fix: pass needed data as constructor parameters, or use a post-construction init step.
scenarios.hint: What parts of the object exist at the moment the base constructor body runs?

scenarios.title: The private inheritance surprise
scenarios.situation: A class inherits from a base with the default inheritance access, and suddenly public base methods are unreachable from outside.
scenarios.prompt: What does the inheritance access specifier control?
choices: class defaults to private inheritance, making all inherited members private — write class Cache : public Store to model is-a
Inheritance is always public in C++ — the error must come from lookup being private in Store
Private inheritance is illegal — use composition instead, always
The access specifier only affects data members, not functions
scenarios.why: The access specifier on inheritance caps the accessibility of inherited members: private inheritance (the default for class, unlike struct) makes public/protected base members private in the derived class. Public inheritance models is-a; private inheritance models implemented-in-terms-of and is rare — composition is usually clearer.
scenarios.hint: What is the default inheritance access for class versus struct, and what does it do to inherited public members?

scenarios.title: The interface that cannot be built
scenarios.situation: A team designs a plugin interface as an abstract base, but a developer tries to instantiate it directly and gets a compile error.
scenarios.prompt: How do pure virtual functions define an interface, and what must a concrete plugin do?
choices: A pure virtual function (= 0) makes the class abstract — concrete plugins must override every pure virtual to become instantiable
= 0 deletes the function — derived classes cannot provide an implementation
Abstract classes cannot have data members — remove them to instantiate
The error means the vtable is missing — link against the plugin library
scenarios.why: = 0 declares a pure virtual function with no required implementation in the base, making the class abstract — it can be used as a pointer/reference type but never instantiated. A derived class becomes concrete only once it overrides all inherited pure virtuals. (A pure virtual can still have a definition that derived classes call explicitly.)
scenarios.hint: What does = 0 say about who must provide the implementation?

scenarios.title: The Missing Virtual Destructor
scenarios.situation: A plugin system holds `std::vector<Base*>` where Derived classes allocate buffers in their constructors and free them in their destructors. `Base` has virtual methods but a non-virtual destructor. Memory profiling shows a steady leak proportional to plugin reloads.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause and fix?
choices: The vector should store unique_ptr<Base> instead of raw pointers
Deleting through a Base* with a non-virtual destructor invokes only ~Base(), so Derived's buffer is never freed — make ~Base() virtual
Derived destructors should be public instead of the current access level
The leak is in the vector reallocation; call shrink_to_fit()
scenarios.why: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer without a virtual destructor is undefined behavior in practice manifesting as a skipped derived destructor — the buffer leaks every reload. unique_ptr (A) is good hygiene but doesn't fix the destructor dispatch. This is the canonical interview question: any class designed as a polymorphic base needs a virtual (or protected non-virtual) destructor.
scenarios.hint: Which destructor actually runs when you delete through the base pointer?

scenarios.title: Slicing in the Event Queue
scenarios.situation: An event system declares `std::vector<Event> queue;` and pushes `MouseEvent` and `KeyEvent` derived objects into it. At dispatch time, `dynamic_cast` checks fail and derived-specific data (coordinates, key codes) is garbage. The virtual dispatch table looks correct in the debugger.
scenarios.prompt: What happened to the derived objects?
choices: The vtable pointer was corrupted by the vector reallocation
Object slicing: vector<Event> stores only the Event subobject — the derived parts were sliced off at push_back; store pointers (smart) or use std::variant
dynamic_cast doesn't work on vector elements
The derived classes need to redeclare the virtual functions
scenarios.why: A `vector<Event>` holds Events, period — pushing a Derived copies only the Base subobject (slicing), discarding derived data and dynamic type. The vtable is fine; there's just no derived object left to dispatch on. Polymorphic collections must hold (smart) pointers or a variant. This is a favorite interview trap because the code compiles cleanly.
scenarios.hint: What does vector<Event> physically store — Events or something else?

scenarios.title: The iterator that died on push_back
scenarios.situation: A loop holds an iterator into a vector while appending new elements. After a few iterations it reads garbage.
scenarios.prompt: Why did the iterator become invalid?
choices: push_back can reallocate the vector's storage, invalidating all iterators, pointers, and references — refresh them after any mutating operation
Iterators are single-use — a vector iterator cannot be dereferenced twice
push_back invalidates only const_iterators — use a mutable iterator
The loop bound is wrong — iterators expire after 512 uses
scenarios.why: A vector stores elements contiguously; when push_back exceeds capacity it allocates a bigger buffer and moves everything, leaving old iterators dangling. The rule: any operation that may reallocate (push_back, insert, reserve beyond capacity) invalidates iterators. Call v.reserve(n) up front when the final size is known, or re-acquire iterators after mutation.
scenarios.hint: Where do the elements physically live after the vector outgrows its buffer?

scenarios.title: The lookup that inserts
scenarios.situation: A read-only statistics pass over a map mysteriously grows it, and a const-incorrect function fails to compile.
scenarios.prompt: What does operator[] do on a missing key?
choices: operator[] default-constructs a value for missing keys and inserts it — use find() or at() for non-inserting lookup
operator[] throws std::out_of_range on missing keys — the growth is from another thread
Maps auto-vivify only for int values — string values are safe
The insertion happens because counts is not const — const maps do not insert
scenarios.why: map::operator[] is specified to insert a value-initialized element when the key is absent — convenient for counting, surprising for lookups. For read-only access use find() (returns end() if missing) or at() (throws out_of_range). Note operator[] cannot even be called on a const map, which is a hint about its mutating nature.
scenarios.hint: Is operator[] a const member function? What does that tell you about what it may do?

scenarios.title: The remove that removed nothing
scenarios.situation: A cleanup pass calls std::remove to drop expired sessions from a vector, but size() is unchanged afterward.
scenarios.prompt: Why did the vector not shrink?
evidence:
std::remove(v.begin(), v.end(), expired);  // elements shifted, size unchanged!
// v.erase(std::remove(...), v.end()); is the full idiom
choices: std::remove only rearranges — it returns the new logical end; you must erase() that range (the erase-remove idiom) to actually shrink the container
std::remove requires a sorted range — sort first
remove works only on lists — vectors need manual loops
The predicate form is std::remove_if — std::remove compares addresses
scenarios.why: Algorithms operate on iterator ranges, not containers — std::remove cannot change v's size, so it compacts the kept elements to the front and returns the new logical end. The erase-remove idiom, v.erase(std::remove(...), v.end()), erases the leftover tail. (C++20's std::erase(v, value) does both in one call.)
scenarios.hint: Can an algorithm that only sees iterators change the container's size? What must it return instead?

scenarios.title: The custom key the hash table rejected
scenarios.situation: Switching a std::map to std::unordered_map for speed fails to compile with a struct key.
scenarios.prompt: What does unordered_map need that map does not?
evidence:
struct Key { int a, b; };
std::unordered_map<Key, int> m;  // error: no hash function for Key
choices: A hash function — specialize std::hash<Key> or pass a custom hasher, plus operator== for equality
Keys must be trivially copyable — add a static_assert instead
unordered_map requires sorted keys — provide operator<
Struct keys are forbidden — pack the fields into a string key
scenarios.why: Ordered map needs only operator<; unordered_map needs a hash (to pick a bucket) and equality (to resolve collisions). The standard pattern is specializing std::hash<Key> to combine member hashes (e.g., h1 ^ (h2 + 0x9e3779b9 + (h1<<6) + (h1>>2))) and defining operator==. Forgetting == compiles but misbehaves on collisions.
scenarios.hint: How does a hash table locate a key — and what two operations does that require of the key type?

scenarios.title: The comparator that crashed sort
scenarios.situation: std::sort with a custom 'less-or-equal' comparator crashes or produces garbage on some inputs.
scenarios.prompt: What contract must a sort comparator satisfy?
evidence: std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](auto a, auto b){ return a <= b; });  // UB: not strict
choices: Strict weak ordering: comp(a,a) must be false — use < (or >), never <=
Comparators must be function pointers — lambdas are not allowed
std::sort requires a total order — provide == as well
The comparator must return int, not bool — return -1/0/1
scenarios.why: std::sort requires a strict weak ordering: irreflexive (comp(a,a) is false), transitive, and antisymmetric. <= violates irreflexivity, which corrupts the algorithm's internal assumptions — undefined behavior, often manifesting as crashes on larger inputs. < (or a proper multi-field lexicographic comparison) satisfies the contract.
scenarios.hint: What should comp(x, x) return — and what does <= return for it?

scenarios.title: The view that outlived its string
scenarios.situation: A function returns a std::string_view into a temporary std::string. Callers read garbage intermittently.
scenarios.prompt: Why is the view dangling?
choices: string_view is a non-owning view — the underlying string is destroyed at function exit, leaving a dangling view; return std::string by value instead
string_view copies the data — the bug is substr returning a view of a view
Returning views is forbidden — string_view can only be a parameter type
fetch() returns a temporary — assign it to a static local to extend its life
scenarios.why: std::string_view holds a pointer and length into someone else's characters; it extends no lifetimes. Returning a view of a local string is the same dangling-pointer bug in modern dress. string_view shines as a function parameter (accepting string, literal, or view without copying), but ownership must outlive the view — return an owning std::string when the data is created inside.
scenarios.hint: Does string_view own the characters it looks at? What happens to those characters when the function returns?

scenarios.title: vector vs list in the Hot Loop
scenarios.situation: A particle simulation stores 2M particles in std::list because 'insertion is O(1)'. The update loop iterates all particles each frame and runs 3x slower than the prototype that used a plain array. Profiling shows the time in pointer chasing, not in the physics math.
scenarios.prompt: What container decision fixes the performance?
choices: Keep std::list but reserve capacity upfront
Switch to std::vector: contiguous storage makes iteration cache-friendly; the O(1) list insertion never mattered because the loop is iteration-bound
Use std::deque for a compromise
Store particles in std::map keyed by ID for faster lookup
scenarios.why: The workload is iterate-all-every-frame: vector's contiguous layout streams through cache lines while list nodes scatter across the heap (pointer chasing + allocation overhead). list's O(1) insertion is irrelevant when nothing inserts mid-frame. list has no reserve (A is a trap — that member doesn't exist); deque helps at the ends but fragments similarly; map adds log-n overhead to a linear scan.
scenarios.hint: What does the loop actually do — insert, or iterate?

scenarios.title: Iterator Invalidation Crash
scenarios.situation: A server loop iterates a std::vector<Connection> and erases timed-out connections inside the loop with `v.erase(it)`. It crashes intermittently under load but never in unit tests. The crash is a heap-use-after-free in the sanitizer.
scenarios.prompt: What is the bug and the idiomatic fix?
choices: The vector needs a mutex around the loop
erase() invalidates the iterator (and all after it on reallocation/shift); use the erase-remove idiom or `it = v.erase(it)` which returns the next valid iterator
Reserve more capacity so erase never reallocates
Switch to indexing with operator[] instead of iterators
scenarios.why: `erase` invalidates the erased iterator (and following ones as elements shift); continuing to `++it` is use-after-invalidation — intermittent because it depends on timing/size. The idiomatic fixes: assign the return value (`it = v.erase(it)`) or erase-remove for predicate-based removal. A mutex (A) addresses threads, not invalidation; reserve (C) doesn't stop the shift; indexing (D) has the same invalidation problem.
scenarios.hint: What does erase() return, and why would it bother?

scenarios.title: The copy that will not compile
scenarios.situation: A factory returns std::unique_ptr<Widget>. A developer tries to store it in two places and gets a deleted-function error.
scenarios.prompt: What does the compile error teach about unique_ptr?
choices: unique_ptr models exclusive ownership — it is movable but not copyable; std::move transfers ownership, leaving the source null
unique_ptr cannot be stored in containers — use raw pointers in vectors
make_widget returns a reference — the copy fails on the reference, not the pointer
The error means Widget is abstract — check the class definition
scenarios.why: unique_ptr's copy operations are deleted precisely to make accidental shared ownership a compile error. Moving transfers the pointer and nulls the source, so exactly one owner exists at a time. Needing two owners is the signal to reach for shared_ptr instead.
scenarios.hint: If two unique_ptrs owned the same object, who would delete it? What does the type system do to prevent that?

scenarios.title: The objects that never die
scenarios.situation: Two objects hold shared_ptrs to each other. Their destructors never run and memory grows over time.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the reference count never reach zero, and what breaks the cycle?
choices: Each object keeps the other alive — a reference cycle; make one link a std::weak_ptr, which observes without owning
shared_ptr requires manual reset — call a->next.reset() before destruction
Cycles are impossible with make_shared — one of the pointers must be raw
The destructors are not virtual — add virtual ~Node()
scenarios.why: shared_ptr destroys its object when the last owner goes away, but in a cycle every object has an owner inside the cycle — the count never drops to zero. weak_ptr holds a non-owning reference: it can lock() to a temporary shared_ptr when access is needed, and it does not keep the target alive. Parent→child owns (shared), child→parent observes (weak) is the classic arrangement.
scenarios.hint: Who owns whom in the cycle — and which of those links actually needs to own?

scenarios.title: The array deleted wrong
scenarios.situation: An array allocated with new[] is freed with scalar delete. Destructors for elements past the first never run.
scenarios.prompt: Why must new[] pair with delete[]?
evidence:
Widget* ws = new Widget[10];
delete ws;  // UB: should be delete[] ws
choices: new[] stores the element count for delete[] to destroy every element — scalar delete destroys only the first and corrupts the heap metadata
delete on arrays leaks the count prefix — the fix is delete[] which the compiler inserts automatically
Scalar delete works for arrays of trivial types — the bug only matters for Widget's members
new[] and delete are interchangeable — the missing destructors are a compiler optimization
scenarios.why: new[] records how many objects were constructed (typically in a hidden prefix) so delete[] can run every destructor and free the right block. Scalar delete assumes a single object: it skips the other destructors and misreads the heap metadata — undefined behavior. Modern guidance: avoid new[] entirely in favor of std::vector or std::make_unique<Widget[]>(10).
scenarios.hint: How would scalar delete know how many destructors to run?

scenarios.title: The mutex left locked on exception
scenarios.situation: A function locks a mutex manually, and an early return on an error path — plus a thrown exception on another — leaves it locked forever.
scenarios.prompt: Which RAII type makes the unlock automatic?
choices: std::lock_guard<std::mutex> — locks on construction, unlocks on destruction, on every exit path including exceptions
std::unique_lock with try_lock — manual control is safer than RAII
std::atomic<bool> flag — replace the mutex with a spin flag
Wrap the body in try/catch and unlock in the catch — RAII does not apply to mutexes
scenarios.why: RAII ties resource release to object lifetime: the lock_guard's destructor runs when the scope exits for any reason — return, exception, or fall-through — so the mutex cannot be left locked. Manual lock/unlock must be duplicated on every path, and one missed path deadlocks the program. (unique_lock adds deferred/try semantics when needed.)
scenarios.hint: What runs when a stack object goes out of scope — even via an exception?

scenarios.title: The object used after the move
scenarios.situation: After std::move-ing a vector into a function, the caller reads the source vector expecting the old data. Sometimes it is empty, sometimes not.
scenarios.prompt: What state is a moved-from object in?
choices: Valid but unspecified — you may only destroy it or assign a new value; reading its old contents is a logic error
Moved-from objects are null — v is guaranteed empty
std::move destroys the source — any use after is undefined behavior
The source keeps its data — move is just a cast with no runtime effect
scenarios.why: std::move is a cast to an rvalue reference; the move constructor then steals the source's resources. The standard guarantees only that a moved-from object is in a valid, destructible state — for vector it is typically empty, but that is not contractual. The safe operations are destruction and assignment of a fresh value.
scenarios.hint: What does the standard promise about a moved-from object — its old value, or merely that it is safe to destroy and reassign?

scenarios.title: The leak between new and the smart pointer
scenarios.situation: A function call like take(std::unique_ptr<Widget>(new Widget), priority()) can leak if priority() throws.
scenarios.prompt: Why is the raw new dangerous here, and what replaces it?
evidence:
take(std::unique_ptr<Widget>(new Widget), priority());
// if priority() throws after new but before the unique_ptr is built: leak
choices: Argument evaluation order is unspecified — std::make_unique<Widget>() builds the object inside the smart pointer with no window for a leak
new never throws — the leak scenario is impossible in practice
unique_ptr's constructor is explicit — the code should not compile at all
Wrap the call in try/catch and delete manually in the catch block
scenarios.why: The compiler may evaluate new Widget, then priority(), then the unique_ptr constructor — if priority() throws in between, the raw pointer is lost and leaks. std::make_unique performs the allocation directly into the smart pointer's control path, eliminating the window. It is also shorter and exception-safe by construction. (make_shared additionally fuses the object and control block into one allocation.)
scenarios.hint: In what order must the three pieces (new, priority(), unique_ptr construction) be evaluated — and is that order guaranteed?

scenarios.title: shared_ptr Cycle in the Scene Graph
scenarios.situation: A scene graph uses shared_ptr for parent->child and child->parent links. Nodes are removed from the scene but memory never drops — the allocator shows every removed subtree still alive. Reference counts on removed nodes stay at 1+.
scenarios.prompt: What is the leak mechanism and the fix?
choices: shared_ptr is broken; switch everything to raw pointers
Reference cycle: parent and child keep each other alive; make the child->parent link a weak_ptr (non-owning back-reference)
Call reset() on every pointer at removal time
The allocator is fragmenting; switch allocators
scenarios.why: shared_ptr cycles never reach zero — parent owns child, child owns parent, so removal from the scene leaves the cycle self-sustaining. weak_ptr expresses the non-owning back-reference: it observes without keeping alive (lock() to use). Manual reset (C) fights the ownership model instead of fixing it; raw pointers (A) abandon safety; the allocator (D) is innocent.
scenarios.hint: Who owns whom — and does the back-link need to own?

scenarios.title: unique_ptr Array Gotcha
scenarios.situation: Legacy code does `std::unique_ptr<Widget> p(new Widget[100]);` and fills the array. It runs fine in tests but corrupts the heap on destruction in production builds. The team debates whether unique_ptr is 'safe for arrays'.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong and what is the correct modern form?
choices: unique_ptr can't manage arrays at all; use new/delete manually
Wrong specialization: unique_ptr<Widget> calls delete, not delete[], on an array — use unique_ptr<Widget[]> (or better, std::vector<Widget>)
The heap corruption is from filling the array, not the deletion
Add a custom deleter that calls delete[]
scenarios.why: `unique_ptr<T>` uses `delete`; arrays need `delete[]` — mismatching them is undefined behavior (the heap corruption on destruction). The `unique_ptr<T[]>` partial specialization uses `delete[]` and even provides operator[]. A custom deleter (D) works but is obsolete; manual new/delete (A) surrenders the safety; and in practice std::vector is usually the right answer over a managed raw array.
scenarios.hint: Which delete does unique_ptr<T> call — and which does an array need?

scenarios.title: The template that copies
scenarios.situation: A generic max function takes its parameters by value because the author wrote template<typename T> without references, silently copying large objects at every call.
scenarios.prompt: How do you write the template to avoid copies while keeping deduction?
evidence:
template <typename T>
T const& max(T const& a, T const& b) { return a < b ? b : a; }  // references: no copies
choices: Take parameters as T const& — deduction still works from the arguments, and no copies occur
Templates cannot deduce reference types — write overloads for each type instead
Use T&& for all parameters — universal references never copy
Deduction only works by value — accept the copies as the cost of genericity
scenarios.why: Template argument deduction works from the argument types regardless of whether the parameter is T, T&, or T const& — the parameter form only controls how the argument binds. T const& binds without copying and accepts temporaries, which is why the standard library's generic algorithms take their arguments this way.
scenarios.hint: Does the choice between T and T const& change what T deduces to — or only how the argument is bound?

scenarios.title: The callback that captures a corpse
scenarios.situation: A function registers a callback capturing a local config by reference. The callback fires after the function returns and reads garbage.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the capture, and when is by-reference capture safe?
choices: [&] captures locals by reference — the reference dangles after setup() returns; capture by value [=] (or move the config in) when the lambda outlives the scope
Lambdas cannot capture locals at all — make cfg a global
By-reference capture copies the value — the bug is in apply(), not the capture
The callback must be invoked synchronously — async callbacks are unsupported
scenarios.why: A reference capture stores a reference to the local variable, not its value — it dangles exactly like a returned pointer to a local. By-reference capture is safe only when the lambda is used within the captured variables' lifetime (e.g., passed to std::sort). For callbacks that outlive the scope, capture by value ([=] or explicit [cfg]) or move ownership in with init-capture ([cfg = std::move(cfg)]).
scenarios.hint: Does [&] store the value of cfg, or a way to reach the local variable — and how long does that variable live?

scenarios.title: The computation that could run at compile time
scenarios.situation: A lookup table is computed at program startup on every run, adding measurable latency, though all inputs are constants.
scenarios.prompt: How do you move the computation to compile time?
evidence:
constexpr int factorial(int n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * factorial(n - 1); }
constexpr int table[] = { factorial(0), factorial(1), factorial(2) };  // built at compile time
choices: Mark the function constexpr and use it in a constant expression — the compiler evaluates it during compilation
const implies compile-time evaluation — the existing const table already does this
Use a macro to compute the values — only the preprocessor runs at compile time
Compile-time computation requires template metaprogramming — rewrite with recursive templates
scenarios.why: constexpr permits a function to be evaluated at compile time when called with constant expressions, and requires it to be usable there. Used in a constant-expression context (like an array bound or constexpr variable initializer), the computation happens during compilation — zero startup cost. const alone only promises not to mutate, not when the value is computed.
scenarios.hint: Which keyword both allows compile-time evaluation and, in the right context, requires it?

scenarios.title: The template error novel
scenarios.situation: A misuse of a generic serializer produces 200 lines of template errors mentioning internals the caller never touched.
scenarios.prompt: How do C++20 concepts improve this?
choices: Concepts constrain the template parameters — violations are diagnosed at the call site with the concept name instead of deep instantiation errors
Concepts make templates run faster — the error output is just shorter as a side effect
The concept replaces the function body — serialize() is auto-generated
Concepts are comments — they have no effect on error messages
scenarios.why: Without constraints, a template's requirements surface only when the body is instantiated, deep in library internals. A concept checks the requirements at the point of use and reports the unsatisfied named requirement ('does not satisfy Serializable'), turning a 200-line error novel into a one-line diagnosis. Concepts also document the interface a type must provide.
scenarios.hint: Where would you rather learn about the misuse — at the call you wrote, or inside the library's implementation?

scenarios.title: The undefined reference to the template
scenarios.situation: A function template is declared in a header and defined in a .cpp file. Linking a caller in another file fails with 'undefined reference'.
scenarios.prompt: Why can the linker not find the template definition?
evidence: template <typename T> T twice(T x);  // declaration only
template <typename T> T twice(T x) { return x + x; }  // invisible to other TUs
choices: Templates are instantiated at compile time per translation unit — the definition must be visible where it is used, so define templates in headers (or explicitly instantiate the needed types)
Template definitions in .cpp files are illegal — the code should not compile
The linker needs --allow-templates to resolve template symbols
twice<int> was never declared — add a non-template overload
scenarios.why: A template is not code — it is a pattern the compiler instantiates per translation unit when it sees a use with concrete arguments. If the definition is hidden in another .cpp, the caller's TU cannot generate twice<int>, and the linker finds nothing. The standard fix is header-only definitions; explicit instantiation (template int twice<int>(int);) works when the type set is closed and known.
scenarios.hint: When is twice<int> actually generated — at the call site's compile, or at link time?

scenarios.title: The lambda that works on any container
scenarios.situation: A logging helper is written three times — once for vector<int>, once for list<string>, once for deque<double> — differing only in types.
scenarios.prompt: How does a generic lambda collapse the three copies?
choices: auto parameters make the lambda's operator() a template — each call instantiates it for the argument's type
auto in lambdas performs type erasure — one runtime function handles all types
The lambda is a macro — the preprocessor generates the three versions
Generic lambdas require C++20 concepts — this only compiles with a concept constraint
scenarios.why: Since C++14, auto in a lambda parameter list makes the call operator a function template; each distinct argument type triggers an instantiation. One generic lambda replaces N overloads, with full type checking per instantiation — unlike macros, with none of the textual-substitution hazards.
scenarios.hint: What does the compiler generate for a lambda whose parameter is auto — one function, or one per call type?

scenarios.title: Template Bloat in the Math Library
scenarios.situation: A header-only math library templates everything on the scalar type. The binary grew 40MB and builds take 25 minutes — profiling shows hundreds of instantiations of identical logic differing only in float vs double vs long double. Most functions don't actually depend on the scalar type's exact width.
scenarios.prompt: How do you cut the bloat without losing genericity?
choices: Stop using templates and write three copies of each function
Factor type-independent logic into non-template base functions (or a common implementation), keep templates as thin wrappers; explicitly instantiate only the needed types in one TU
Mark everything inline to help the linker
Split the header into more headers
scenarios.why: Template bloat comes from instantiating identical machine code per type — hoisting the type-independent core into a regular function means one copy, with thin template shims for the type-dependent surface; explicit instantiation in a single translation unit prevents N copies across TUs. Manual copies (A) are unmaintainable; inline (C) can worsen bloat; more headers (D) doesn't change instantiation count.
scenarios.hint: Which parts of the logic actually care whether it's float or double?
evidence: Hoists common logic out of templates

scenarios.title: Lambda Capture Dangling Reference
scenarios.situation: A function builds a task queue: `for (auto& job : jobs) queue.push([&]{ process(job); });` The queue runs after the function returns. Intermittently, jobs process with garbage data or crash. Capturing by value `[=]` 'fixes' it but copies large job objects.
scenarios.prompt: What is the bug and the efficient fix?
choices: Lambdas can't be stored; run them immediately instead
[&] captures job by reference — after the loop/function ends the reference dangles; capture the needed data by value with an init-capture move: `[j = std::move(job)]` (or capture a shared_ptr)
Make job a global variable
Add a mutex around the queue
scenarios.why: Default reference capture `[&]` stores references to loop variables that die when the function returns — classic dangling. `[=]` copies (safe but expensive for large jobs). Init-capture with move (`[j = std::move(job)]`) transfers ownership into the lambda: no dangle, no copy. Globals (C) and mutexes (D) don't address lifetime at all.
scenarios.hint: How long does the captured reference live versus how long does the lambda live?

scenarios.title: Undefined reference to vtable
scenarios.situation: Linking fails with 'undefined reference to vtable for Widget' even though every declared method seems defined.
scenarios.prompt: What usually causes this linker error?
choices: The first non-inline virtual function lacks a definition — the compiler emits the vtable where that function is defined, so define every virtual (often = default the destructor in a .cpp)
Vtables require RTTI — compile with -frtti explicitly
The class needs a virtual base — add : virtual public Base
Linkers cannot handle virtual functions — replace with function pointers
scenarios.why: The compiler emits a class's vtable in the translation unit containing the definition of its first non-inline virtual function (the 'key function'). If that function is declared but never defined — commonly a forgotten virtual destructor — no TU emits the vtable and the link fails. Defining the destructor (even as = default in the .cpp) anchors the vtable.
scenarios.hint: In which translation unit does the compiler place the vtable — and what determines that choice?

scenarios.title: The function defined in two files
scenarios.situation: A small helper is defined in a header included by two .cpp files. The linker reports a multiple-definition error.
scenarios.prompt: How do you share a function definition via a header?
evidence: int clamp(int v, int lo, int hi) { return v < lo ? lo : (v > hi ? hi : v); }  // in header
choices: Mark it inline (or make it a template/constexpr) — inline permits identical definitions in multiple translation units
Headers may only declare functions — move the body to one .cpp file
Add static so each TU gets its own copy — identical behavior, no link error
The linker flag --allow-duplicate-functions resolves it
scenarios.why: The one-definition rule allows only one definition of a non-inline function program-wide. inline explicitly permits the same definition in multiple TUs (the linker merges them) — it is the mechanism for header-defined helpers, and modern compilers also use it as an inlining hint. static would instead create separate copies per TU (bloat, and distinct addresses).
scenarios.hint: Which keyword tells the linker that identical definitions across translation units are intentional, not an error?

scenarios.title: The include path that leaked
scenarios.situation: A CMake project sets global include_directories(), and an unrelated target starts picking up the wrong headers after a dependency is added.
scenarios.prompt: What is the modern CMake alternative?
evidence:
include_directories(${DEPS}/include)  # global: affects every target
add_executable(app main.cpp)
add_library(util util.cpp)  # also sees DEPS headers: wrong
choices: target_include_directories(app PRIVATE ...) — properties attach to specific targets with PUBLIC/PRIVATE/INTERFACE scoping instead of polluting everything
Global settings are the CMake way — pin the dependency version to avoid conflicts
Set the include path as an environment variable instead of in CMake
Merge all targets into one executable so the leak does not matter
scenarios.why: Directory-scoped commands like include_directories() affect every target defined after them — action at a distance. Modern CMake is target-based: target_include_directories (and target_link_libraries, target_compile_features) attach usage requirements to one target, with PRIVATE (build only), PUBLIC (build + consumers), and INTERFACE (consumers only) controlling propagation precisely.
scenarios.hint: Which CMake commands apply to one named target, and which ones spray settings across the whole directory?

scenarios.title: The CI check that finds memory bugs
scenarios.situation: A C++ service has intermittent heap corruption in production. The team wants CI to catch such bugs before merge.
scenarios.prompt: Which build flags give the best automated memory-error detection?
evidence:
clang++ -std=c++20 -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g -o tests *.cpp
./tests  # aborts with symbolicated trace on first error
choices: -fsanitize=address,undefined with -g — ASan finds overflows/use-after-free, UBSan finds UB like signed overflow, with precise stack traces
-O3 alone — the optimizer eliminates undefined behavior automatically
-static analysis via -Wall — warnings catch all runtime memory errors
Run the tests under strace — system call traces reveal heap corruption
scenarios.why: AddressSanitizer instruments memory accesses to catch heap/stack/global overflows, use-after-free, and leaks (with LeakSanitizer); UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer catches signed-integer overflow, bad shifts, misaligned access, and null dereference. Together at ~2x slowdown they are the highest-signal automated memory check available — far beyond what warnings alone can prove.
scenarios.hint: Which tools observe the program as it actually runs, rather than reasoning about the source?

scenarios.title: The warning that became a bug
scenarios.situation: A sign-comparison warning scrolled past in a long build log and shipped; it was a real out-of-bounds read on 32-bit builds.
scenarios.prompt: How do you make warnings impossible to ignore?
choices: Build with -Werror so warnings fail the build, and keep -Wall -Wextra (-Wconversion for extra strictness) — CI stays warning-clean by construction
Warnings are advisory — schedule a quarterly warning-review meeting instead
-w suppresses warnings so logs stay readable — fewer warnings means fewer bugs
Only -Wall is needed — -Wextra and -Werror add no value
scenarios.why: -Werror elevates every warning to a build failure, so no warning can scroll past unnoticed — the codebase stays warning-clean by construction. -Wall -Wextra enable the high-signal diagnostics (sign compare, unused, shadowing); -Wconversion adds implicit-conversion warnings for stricter codebases. The discipline only works if the team fixes warnings instead of locally disabling them.
scenarios.hint: What turns 'the compiler noticed something suspicious' into 'the build refuses to proceed'?

scenarios.title: The library that linked backwards
scenarios.situation: Linking fails with undefined references to a static library's symbols, even though the library is listed on the command line.
scenarios.prompt: Why does static library order matter on the link line?
evidence:
g++ -o app -lutil main.cpp   # fails: undefined reference
# g++ -o app main.cpp -lutil  # works
choices: The linker resolves static libraries left-to-right in a single pass — libraries must come after the objects that reference them
-lutil must come first as a dependency declaration — the working order is a coincidence
Static libraries cannot satisfy references from .cpp files — use shared libraries
The library was built with a different compiler — rebuild everything
scenarios.why: Traditional Unix linkers make one left-to-right pass: when they encounter a static archive they pull in only the members that resolve currently-undefined symbols. If -lutil appears before main.cpp, no symbols are undefined yet, so nothing is pulled in — then main.cpp's references go unresolved. Dependents before dependencies, always; or use --start-group/--end-group (or CMake, which orders for you).
scenarios.hint: When the linker meets the archive, which symbols are currently undefined — and which does it extract?

scenarios.title: The ODR Violation That Only Fails on Fridays
scenarios.situation: A function behaves differently in debug vs release, and differently again when a new TU is added. Investigation finds a non-inline function defined in a header included by 12 TUs, with slightly different macro settings per TU. The linker never complained.
scenarios.prompt: What rule is violated and what is the fix?
choices: The One Definition Rule: a non-inline function defined in a header creates 12 differing definitions (linker picks one silently); mark it inline, or move the definition to one .cpp with a declaration in the header
The build needs -O0 everywhere for consistency
Headers should never contain function bodies
It's a compiler bug; upgrade the toolchain
scenarios.why: ODR requires exactly one definition of a non-inline function program-wide — a header definition included in 12 TUs with different macros yields 12 different definitions, and the linker silently keeps one (no diagnostic required). `inline` explicitly permits multiple identical definitions; otherwise define once in a .cpp. -O0 (B) masks it; 'never bodies in headers' (C) is overbroad (inline/template bodies are fine).
scenarios.hint: Twelve translation units, twelve definitions, zero linker errors — which rule allows the linker to stay silent?
evidence: Moves definition to single TU or inline

scenarios.title: Link Order Linker Errors
scenarios.situation: Linking fails with 'undefined reference to Logger::write' although liblogging.a definitely contains the symbol (verified with nm). The link command lists `-llogging` BEFORE the object files that use it. Reordering fixes it, but nobody understands why.
scenarios.prompt: Why does library order matter with static linking?
choices: The linker is buggy and order shouldn't matter
Traditional Unix linkers process left-to-right, pulling from a static archive only the objects resolving currently-undefined symbols — a library before its users contributes nothing
liblogging.a was built with the wrong architecture
nm shows symbols the linker can't see due to visibility settings
scenarios.why: Static archives are lazy symbol pools: the linker scans left to right, and when it reaches liblogging.a it only extracts members satisfying undefined symbols seen SO FAR. Listed first, there are no undefined symbols yet, so nothing is extracted — later objects' references stay unresolved. Hence: libraries after the objects that need them (or use --start-group). Shared libraries don't behave this way, which is why the confusion is common.
scenarios.hint: What does the linker know at the moment it opens the archive?

scenarios.title: The Core Syntax Mystery

scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Core Syntax?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Core Syntax issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Core Syntax is too complex to troubleshoot systematically

(3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: Compilation Pipeline: Where Did My Symbol Go?
scenarios.situation: A build fails at link time: 'undefined reference to Config::load()'. The .cpp file compiles cleanly, the header declares it, and the object file exists. The pipeline stages are: preprocess -> compile -> assemble -> link.
scenarios.prompt: Which stage is failing and what does that tell you about the cause?
choices: Compile stage: the function body has a syntax error

Link stage: compilation succeeded (object file exists), so the definition isn't reaching the linker — the .cpp isn't in the build, or the signature/mangling mismatches (e.g., namespace or const mismatch)
Preprocess stage: the header guard is broken
Assemble stage: the assembler dropped the symbol
scenarios.why: Clean compilation proves preprocessing, compiling, and assembling all succeeded — the symbol is missing at link time, meaning the definition's object file isn't linked in, or the mangled name differs (namespace, parameter types, or const-qualification mismatch between declaration and definition). Syntax (A) would fail compilation; header guards (C) would break compilation too; assemblers (D) don't drop symbols.
scenarios.hint: The object file exists — so which stages already proved themselves innocent?
evidence: Isolates missing definition at link stage

scenarios.title: Memory Layout: The Corrupted Global
scenarios.situation: A global `int config_value = 42;` reads as 0 at startup on an embedded target, while a global `int counter;` (uninitialized) reads garbage instead of 0. The startup code was recently 'optimized'.
scenarios.prompt: Using program memory layout (.text / .data / .bss / stack / heap), what broke?
choices: The heap allocator is corrupting globals
.data (initialized globals like config_value) isn't being copied from flash, and .bss (zero-initialized, like counter) isn't being zeroed — the CRT startup routine was gutted
Stack overflow is overwriting the globals
The linker script placed .data in RAM that doesn't exist
scenarios.why: Initialized globals live in .data (loaded from the binary image at startup); uninitialized/zero globals live in .bss (zeroed at startup). config_value=0 means .data wasn't copied; garbage counter means .bss wasn't zeroed — both are jobs of the C runtime startup code that runs before main(). The 'optimization' removed it. Heap (A) and stack (C) don't hold globals; a bad linker script (D) would typically fault, not zero.
scenarios.hint: Who is responsible for preparing .data and .bss before main() runs?

scenarios.title: Stack Frames: The Vanishing Return Address
scenarios.situation: A recursive parser crashes with a stack overflow on deeply nested input (10,000 levels). Each frame holds a 4KB parse buffer as a local array. The recursion depth itself is algorithmically necessary.
scenarios.prompt: Following stack-frame anatomy (return address, saved registers, locals), what is the minimal fix?
choices: Increase the thread stack size to 64MB
Move the 4KB buffer off the stack (heap-allocate it or make it a reused member) — frame size, not depth, is the multiplier; 10k frames x small frame fits, x 4KB doesn't
Convert the recursion to iteration
Add a depth counter and throw at 5,000
scenarios.why: Stack usage = depth x frame size. The depth is required, but the 4KB local is not — moving it to the heap (or reusing one buffer) shrinks each frame to tens of bytes, so 10k frames fit comfortably. Bigger stacks (A) just move the cliff; iteration (C) is a bigger rewrite for the same effect; an arbitrary cap (D) rejects valid input.
scenarios.hint: Two factors multiply into stack usage — which one is actually optional here?
objectives: Fix stack overflows by frame size
evidence: Moves large local off the stack

scenarios.title: STL Internals: vector Growth Cliff
scenarios.situation: A latency-sensitive service does `v.push_back(x)` in a loop without reserve(). p99 latency shows periodic 50ms spikes; between spikes it's 50ns per push. The vector holds 10M elements by end of day.
scenarios.prompt: What internal mechanism causes the spikes?
choices: The allocator is fragmenting under load
Geometric growth: when capacity is exhausted, vector allocates a bigger buffer (typically 1.5-2x) and moves all elements — an O(n) reallocation spike, amortized O(1) overall
push_back is O(n) because it shifts elements
The CPU cache is being thrashed by sequential writes
scenarios.why: vector grows geometrically: most push_backs are a cheap write, but each capacity exhaustion triggers allocate + move-N-elements + free — the periodic 50ms cliff, amortized to O(1). The fix is reserve() up front. Allocator fragmentation (A) wouldn't be periodic; push_back doesn't shift (C — that's insert at front); sequential writes (D) are the cache-friendliest pattern there is.
scenarios.hint: Spikes are periodic and the cost between them is tiny — what grows geometrically?

scenarios.title: Linker/Loader Flow: The Slow Startup
scenarios.situation: A C++ application links 80 shared libraries and takes 12 seconds to start — before main() does anything. Profiling the startup shows the time in symbol resolution, and the binary has 200k exported symbols.
scenarios.prompt: Where in the loader flow is the time going, and how do you cut it?
choices: The kernel is slow to mmap 80 libraries; use fewer threads
Dynamic loader symbol relocation: reduce exported symbols (visibility=hidden, version scripts), cut unnecessary library dependencies, consider prelinking/relative relocations
main() is doing too much static initialization
The disk is slow; buy faster storage
scenarios.why: Before main(), the dynamic loader maps libraries and performs relocations — with 200k exported symbols across 80 libs, symbol lookup (hash chains, string compares) dominates. -fvisibility=hidden plus version scripts shrink the dynamic symbol table dramatically; pruning unused DT_NEEDED entries shortens the search. Static init (C) happens after relocation; disk (D) is a one-time map cost, not 12s of symbol work.
scenarios.hint: The time is before main() and scales with symbol count — what does the loader do with symbols?

scenarios.title: Cache Hierarchy: The False Sharing Slowdown
scenarios.situation: Two threads each increment their own counter in a tight loop. The counters are adjacent members of a struct (8 bytes apart). On a 16-core machine the loop runs 5x SLOWER with two threads than one thread does alone. CPU utilization shows both cores busy.
scenarios.prompt: What cache-coherence effect explains this?
choices: The threads are context-switching too often
False sharing: both counters share one 64-byte cache line, so each increment invalidates the line in the other core's cache — cores ping-pong the line instead of computing
The memory bus is saturated by two increment streams
The compiler didn't vectorize the loop
scenarios.why: Cache coherence works at 64-byte line granularity: two counters in one line mean every write by either core invalidates the other's cached copy, forcing a cross-core transfer per increment — the cores serialize on the interconnect. The fix is padding/alignas(64) to put each counter on its own line. Context switches (A) don't apply to pinned busy loops; two increments can't saturate the bus (C); vectorization (D) is irrelevant to scalar counters.
scenarios.hint: Coherence moves 64 bytes at a time — how far apart are the counters?
evidence: Pads counters to separate cache lines
