domains.name: C++ Interview Prep
domains.description: The questions C++ interviews actually ask: ownership, lifetimes, templates, and 'what does this print' traps.

scenarios.title: What Does This Print?
scenarios.prompt: What happens, and why?
choices: Prints 'hello' — the const reference extends the lifetime

Undefined behavior: f returns a reference to a local destroyed at return; r dangles. Lifetime extension does not apply through function returns — the fix is to return by value (NRVO/move makes it free)
Compilation error — cannot return a reference to a local
Prints garbage but is technically defined
scenarios.why: Lifetime extension applies when a temporary is bound directly to a reference in the same scope — NOT through a function return. `s` dies when f() returns; r is a dangling reference and any use is UB (often 'works' in practice, which makes it worse). The fix is return-by-value: NRVO or move makes it zero-cost. This exact trap appears in interviews because it tests whether you trace lifetimes or guess from output.
scenarios.hint: Where does `s` live, and when does it die? Does the reference cross that boundary?
evidence: const std::string& f() { std::string s="hello"; return s; }
Often prints 'hello' in debug builds — UB that looks fine.

scenarios.title: Code Review: The Clever Ternary Chain
scenarios.situation: In a code review you find: `return x > 0 ? (y > 0 ? a : b) : (y > 0 ? c : d);` The author defends it as 'efficient — no branches'. The function is in a billing path that changes quarterly.
scenarios.prompt: What is your review decision?
choices: Approve — fewer branches means faster code
Request changes: rewrite as explicit if/else with named conditions — the ternary chain is unreadable, untestable per-branch, and the compiler generates the same branches anyway
Approve but add a comment explaining the logic
Rewrite it yourself using a lookup table
scenarios.why: Nested ternaries don't eliminate branches — the compiler emits the same comparisons; they only eliminate readability. In a quarterly-changing billing path, the cost is future mis-edits and untestable branches. Request explicit control flow with named booleans. A comment (C) documents confusion instead of removing it; rewriting it yourself (D) bypasses the author's learning.
scenarios.hint: Who pays the cost of this cleverness — the CPU or the next engineer?

scenarios.title: Trade-off: Exceptions vs Error Codes
scenarios.situation: The interviewer asks: 'Your team is writing a high-frequency trading gateway in C++. Do you use exceptions or error codes?' The gateway processes 1M messages/sec; failures are rare but must be handled precisely.
scenarios.prompt: What is the strong interview answer?
choices: Exceptions — modern C++ prefers them and they're cleaner
Error codes (std::expected / status returns): zero-cost on the hot path, deterministic latency with no unwinding; reserve exceptions for truly exceptional, non-performance-critical paths
assert() and crash on any error
Mix randomly per developer preference
scenarios.why: This tests trade-off reasoning, not dogma: exceptions have zero cost when not thrown but unpredictable latency when thrown (unwinding, cache effects) — unacceptable where p99 latency is the product. std::expected makes errors explicit, composable, and free on success. The strong answer names the criterion (deterministic latency) and the exception (use exceptions where latency doesn't matter). assert-and-crash (C) is for invariants, not handleable errors.
scenarios.hint: What is the product actually selling — clean code or predictable nanoseconds?
evidence: Justifies error codes by latency determinism

scenarios.title: Debugging: The Heisenbug That Vanishes
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'A crash reproduces in release but disappears the moment you attach a debugger or add print statements. Walk me through your debugging.' The crash is a segfault in an optimized multithreaded service.
scenarios.prompt: What debugging strategy do you describe?
choices: Keep adding prints until it reproduces under the debugger

Suspect undefined behavior (use-after-free, data race, uninitialized read) whose manifestation depends on timing/layout: run under ASan/TSan/UBSan, capture core dumps with full symbols, and bisect with -O0 vs -O2 to isolate optimizer-sensitive UB
Blame the optimizer and ship -O0
Rewrite the crashing module from scratch
scenarios.why: Heisenbugs that flee observation scream UB or races — timing/layout-dependent. Sanitizers (ASan/TSan/UBSan) detect the bug class directly instead of chasing symptoms; core dumps preserve the optimized crash; optimization-level bisection isolates miscompiled-UB cases. More prints (A) perturbs timing further; -O0 (C) hides it in production; rewrite (D) is surrender without diagnosis.
scenarios.hint: What class of bug changes behavior when you merely observe it?

scenarios.title: Design: Cache for the Config Service
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'Design an in-memory cache for a config service: 10k keys, reads 100k/sec, writes 10/sec, values up to 1MB, must never serve stale data older than 1 second.' They watch how you handle the read/write asymmetry.
scenarios.prompt: What design do you propose?
choices: std::map with a single mutex — simple and correct
Read-optimized: std::unordered_map with shared_mutex (shared_lock for reads, unique_lock for writes), versioned entries with timestamps, background refresh keeping staleness under 1s
Lock-free everything with atomics
Redis — don't build it yourself
scenarios.why: The 10,000:1 read/write ratio demands read-optimized concurrency: shared_mutex lets 100k reads proceed in parallel while rare writes exclude briefly; versioning + timestamps enforce the 1s staleness bound explicitly. A single mutex (A) serializes 100k reads; lock-free (C) is overkill complexity for 10 writes/sec; Redis (D) dodges the design question the interviewer asked.
scenarios.hint: Which operation dominates, and what synchronization shape matches a 10000:1 ratio?

scenarios.title: Behavioral With Teeth: The Production Incident
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'Tell me about a time you caused a production incident.' You once deployed an O(n^2) config parser that took down a service at scale. They're probing ownership and technical depth, not just storytelling.
scenarios.prompt: What makes the answer strong?
choices: Emphasize it wasn't really your fault — the reviewer approved it

STAR with technical depth: what you shipped, the exact failure mode (quadratic blowup at 50k entries), how you detected it, the immediate mitigation, and the systemic fix (load tests with production-scale fixtures + complexity review checklist)
Keep it vague to avoid looking bad
Say you've never caused an incident
scenarios.why: Interviewers score ownership + learning + technical precision: naming the exact mechanism (O(n^2) at 50k entries) proves depth, the mitigation shows calm under pressure, and the systemic fix (scale-realistic load tests, checklist) shows you fixed the process, not just the bug. Deflection (A), vagueness (C), and denial (D) all signal the opposite of what's being tested.
scenarios.hint: They're grading what you changed afterward, not the mistake itself.
evidence: Gives STAR with mechanism + systemic fix

scenarios.title: Rule of Five in the Interview
scenarios.situation: Interviewer shows a class managing a raw buffer with a custom destructor and copy constructor, then asks: 'What else does this class need, and what happens if we add a move constructor but nothing else?'
scenarios.prompt: What is the complete correct answer?
choices: Nothing else — destructor plus copy constructor is sufficient

Rule of five: it also needs copy assignment, move constructor, and move assignment (or =delete the ones you don't want); adding only a move constructor suppresses the copy operations, silently breaking existing copies
Just add a move assignment too
Replace everything with =default
scenarios.why: Managing a resource means owning the full copy/move/destroy set — and the subtle trap: declaring any move operation deletes the copy operations (and vice versa per the rules), so a lone move constructor silently breaks code that copies. The complete answer states the rule of five AND the suppression side-effect. =default (D) on a raw-buffer class would shallow-copy the buffer — the original bug.
scenarios.hint: What does declaring a move constructor do to the copy constructor you didn't declare?
evidence: States rule of five + suppression effects

scenarios.title: Estimating Live: How Much Memory?
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'We store 50 million user sessions in std::unordered_map<std::string, Session>. Roughly how much memory is that, and what's your biggest lever to cut it?' Session is 64 bytes; average key length 20 chars.
scenarios.prompt: What estimation reasoning do you show?
choices: 50M x (64 + 20) bytes = ~4.2GB, and that's the answer

Per-node overhead dominates: node allocation (~32B) + bucket pointer + string's own allocation (~20B + overhead) + 64B session ≈ 150-200B per entry → 8-10GB; biggest lever is a flat_map/sorted vector or string interning to kill per-node and per-key allocations
It depends on the machine, so you can't estimate
Use a bigger hash table to reduce memory
scenarios.why: Interview estimation tests overhead-awareness: unordered_map is node-based (each entry a separate allocation with pointer overhead), and std::string usually heap-allocates — the overhead dwarfs the 84 bytes of payload. Naming the components and the lever (contiguous storage, interning) shows systems thinking. The naive multiply (A) misses 2x overhead; 'can't estimate' (C) forfeits the question; bigger tables (D) increase memory.
scenarios.hint: Count the allocations per entry, not just the bytes of payload.

domains.name: Concurrency & Multithreading
domains.description: Threads, mutexes, atomics, and the memory model — where C++ interviews separate seniors from the rest.

scenarios.title: The Service That Freezes at Midnight
scenarios.situation: A service deadlocks roughly once a night. Two mutexes (db_mutex, cache_mutex) are involved. Thread A locks db then cache; Thread B locks cache then db. It worked for months.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause and the fix?
choices: Race condition in the business logic — add more logging

Classic lock-order inversion: A holds db waits for cache while B holds cache waits for db — circular wait. Fix: establish a global lock order (always db before cache) and enforce it; or use std::lock()/std::scoped_lock to acquire atomically
The mutexes are too slow — replace with spinlocks
Thread starvation — raise thread priorities
scenarios.why: Inconsistent lock ordering is the textbook deadlock: each thread holds one lock and waits for the other — circular wait, one of Coffman's four. 'Worked for months' is normal; deadlock needs the unlucky interleaving. The durable fix is a documented global order (db before cache, everywhere) or atomic multi-acquire (std::scoped_lock locks without deadlock). Logging more will not fix an ordering bug; spinlocks make it spin faster.
scenarios.hint: Draw the wait graph: who holds what, who waits for what? Is there a cycle?
evidence: A: waiting on cache_mutex; B: waiting on db_mutex.

scenarios.title: Race Diagnosis: The Flaky Counter
scenarios.situation: A metrics counter `total_requests++` is incremented from 8 worker threads. The reported total is consistently 5-15% BELOW the true count, and the deficit grows with thread count. No crashes, no sanitizer warnings in the default build.
scenarios.prompt: What is the diagnosis and the minimal fix?
choices: The threads need joining before reading the counter
Data race on non-atomic increment: read-modify-write interleavings lose updates; make it std::atomic<long long> (or a sharded per-thread counter summed at read)
The counter is overflowing; use a bigger type
CPU caches are stale; add a memory barrier manually
scenarios.why: Non-atomic `++` is load-add-store: two threads can load the same value and both store N+1, losing one update — the deficit scales with contention, exactly the symptom. std::atomic makes the increment indivisible (TSan would have flagged it). Joining (A) doesn't fix the race; overflow (C) would show wraparound, not a deficit; manual barriers (D) are what atomics already provide.
scenarios.hint: Three machine instructions, two threads — draw the interleave that loses a count.

scenarios.title: Mutex vs Atomic: The Config Flag
scenarios.situation: A boolean `shutdown_requested` is polled by 32 threads in tight loops and set once by the main thread. A reviewer suggests std::mutex; another suggests std::atomic<bool>; a third says 'bool is one byte, it's already atomic'.
scenarios.prompt: Which is correct and why?
choices: std::mutex — always the safe default

std::atomic<bool>: single flag, trivially copyable — atomics give the needed visibility/ordering with near-zero cost; a mutex per poll would serialize 32 tight loops, and plain bool is a data race regardless of size
Plain bool — single-byte accesses can't tear
volatile bool — it prevents caching
scenarios.why: 'One byte' doesn't mean atomic or visible — without synchronization it's a data race (UB), and the compiler may hoist the read out of the loop entirely. atomic<bool> is the exact tool: lock-free on every major platform, correct visibility, negligible cost. A mutex (A) around a flag poll is massive overkill; volatile (D) is not a synchronization primitive in C++.
scenarios.hint: What stops the compiler from reading the flag once and reusing the value forever?

scenarios.title: Deadlock at 3 AM
scenarios.situation: A service deadlocks roughly weekly. Two mutexes guard the account map (m_accounts) and the audit log (m_audit). Thread 1's transfer path locks accounts then audit; a new reporting path locks audit then accounts. Core dumps show each thread holding one mutex and waiting on the other.
scenarios.prompt: What is the deadlock and the robust fix?
choices: It's a livelock; add random backoff and retry
Classic lock-order inversion (AB-BA deadlock): enforce a global lock ordering (always accounts before audit), or use std::lock/std::scoped_lock to acquire both atomically
Merge the two mutexes into one big lock
Increase the thread stack so the wait doesn't deadlock
scenarios.why: The dump is the textbook AB-BA cycle: T1 holds A waits B, T2 holds B waits A — inconsistent lock ordering. The robust fix is a single global order (documented and enforced) or std::lock/scoped_lock which acquires multiple mutexes deadlock-free. Backoff (A) misdiagnoses deadlock as livelock; one big lock (C) works but serializes unrelated audit writes — acceptable fallback, not the principled fix.
scenarios.hint: Draw who holds what and who waits for what — what shape is it?
evidence: Maps AB-BA cycle and orders locks

scenarios.title: Thread Pool Sizing for the Image Pipeline
scenarios.situation: An image pipeline has two stages: CPU-bound thumbnail generation and I/O-bound cloud upload. The current pool uses 64 threads for everything on a 16-core box. Thumbnails are slow (context switching) and uploads stall (threads blocked on network while thumbnails wait for slots).
scenarios.prompt: How do you size the pools?
choices: One pool of 16 threads for everything — match core count
Two pools: ~16 threads for CPU-bound thumbnails (cores + small headroom), larger pool (e.g., 64+) for I/O-bound uploads where threads mostly wait
256 threads in one pool to keep everything fed
One thread per stage in a pipeline chain
scenarios.why: CPU-bound work wants ~core count (more threads just context-switch); I/O-bound work wants many threads because each spends most of its life blocked, not computing. Separate pools stop blocked upload threads from starving thumbnail slots and vice versa. A single 16-pool (A) underfeeds uploads; 256 (C) thrashes the CPU stage; a 2-thread chain (D) serializes all throughput.
scenarios.hint: What is each thread doing most of the time — computing or waiting?
objectives: Size thread pools by workload type

scenarios.title: Data Race Fix: The Lazy Cache
scenarios.situation: A config cache is lazily built on first use: `if (!cache_) cache_ = build(); return *cache_;` Under load, two threads enter simultaneously, both build, one result leaks, and occasionally a thread reads a half-constructed cache. std::call_once was suggested but 'seems heavy'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct fix?
choices: Double-checked locking with a plain bool flag
std::call_once with std::once_flag — exactly the tool for one-time initialization; or a function-local static (magic statics are thread-safe since C++11)
Build the cache eagerly at startup and skip laziness
Wrap the whole thing in a mutex on every access
scenarios.why: Double-checked locking with a plain flag is broken (the half-constructed read is the classic publication-safety failure). std::call_once exists precisely for this — one-time, race-free, and cheap after the first call. Function-local statics give the same guarantee with less code. Eager init (C) is a fine alternative when startup cost is acceptable; per-access mutex (D) pessimizes the hot path.
scenarios.hint: The half-constructed read is a publication problem — what guarantees safe publication?

scenarios.title: Condition Variable: The Missed Wakeup
scenarios.situation: A worker waits for jobs: `if (queue.empty()) cv.wait(lock); job = queue.pop();` Occasionally it pops from an empty queue and crashes, or sleeps forever despite queued jobs. The notifier does `queue.push(j); cv.notify_one();`.
scenarios.prompt: What are the two bugs and the fix?
choices: notify_one should be notify_all, and the mutex is unnecessary
`if` must be `while` (spurious wakeups + the check-then-wait race), and the predicate check with wait(lock, pred) is the fix: `cv.wait(lock, [&]{ return !queue.empty(); });`
The queue needs to be a priority queue
Wait without holding the lock to avoid deadlock
scenarios.why: Two classic bugs: (1) `if` instead of `while` — spurious wakeups (allowed by the standard) pop an empty queue; (2) the check-then-act race — a job can arrive between empty() and wait(), and the notify fires before wait() sleeps, so it sleeps forever. The predicate form of wait() rechecks atomically under the lock, fixing both. notify_all (A) doesn't fix either; waiting unlocked (D) is itself a race.
scenarios.hint: What happens between the empty() check and the wait() — and what does the standard allow wait() to do spontaneously?

scenarios.title: Lock Granularity: The Contended Registry
scenarios.situation: A service registry uses one mutex guarding a map of 100k services. With 48 threads doing lookups, throughput plateaus at 8 threads and lock contention dominates profiles. Writes (register/unregister) are 0.1% of operations.
scenarios.prompt: What concurrency design unlocks the read throughput?
choices: Remove the mutex — reads don't modify the map
Reader-writer shape: std::shared_mutex with shared_lock for lookups and unique_lock for the rare writes; or sharded maps with per-shard mutexes
A spinlock instead of a mutex for lower latency
Make the map thread-local in each thread
scenarios.why: 99.9% reads means the exclusive mutex serializes work that doesn't conflict — shared_mutex lets concurrent readers proceed while rare writes still exclude. Sharding is the alternative when even reader coordination costs too much. Removing the lock (A) races with the 0.1% writes (and rehashing); spinlocks (C) still serialize; thread-local copies (D) break consistency on writes.
scenarios.hint: What fraction of operations actually conflict with each other?

domains.name: Performance Engineering
domains.description: Measure first, optimize second: profiling, cache behavior, and the optimizations that actually matter.

scenarios.title: The 'Optimized' Code That Got Slower
scenarios.situation: A developer 'optimized' a hot loop with clever bit tricks. Benchmarks show it is 15% SLOWER than the original. The original was a simple loop over a vector.
scenarios.prompt: What likely happened, and what is the correct process?
choices: The compiler is broken — file a bug report

The 'optimization' defeated the compiler: bit tricks can block auto-vectorization and obscure the pattern the optimizer recognizes. Process: profile first, change one thing, benchmark with production flags, keep or revert — the measurement is the verdict, not the cleverness
The CPU is thermal throttling — improve cooling
15% is noise — ship the clever version, it looks better
scenarios.why: Modern compilers vectorize simple loops brilliantly; 'clever' code often hides the pattern and prevents SIMD. The process failure is bigger than the code failure: no baseline measurement, no controlled comparison, optimization by aesthetics. The correct loop is profile → hypothesis → single change → benchmark (same flags, multiple runs) → keep/revert. Cleverness is not a performance strategy; measurement is.
scenarios.hint: What does the compiler do to simple loops? What does 'clever' do to the compiler?
evidence: Original: high vectorization; new: scalar, more branches.

scenarios.title: Reading the Flame Graph
scenarios.situation: A profiler flame graph for a slow request handler shows a wide plateau in `serialize()` taking 60% of samples, with narrow towers for JSON escaping inside it. The team wants to rewrite the JSON library. The handler also does 200 small allocations per request.
scenarios.prompt: What does the flame graph actually tell you to do first?
choices: Rewrite the JSON library — 60% is 60%
Attack the width first: reduce how often serialize() runs (cache serialized output, avoid re-serializing unchanged data); the narrow escaping towers are second-order
Optimize the 200 allocations — allocation is always the bottleneck
Add more threads to parallelize serialization
scenarios.why: Flame graph width = frequency x cost: a wide plateau means the frame runs often and long — the first question is whether the work can be avoided (caching, dirty-checking), which beats optimizing it. Only after eliminating redundant calls do you optimize the escaping towers. Rewriting the library (A) optimizes necessary work before questioning necessity; allocations (C) may matter but the graph says serialize dominates; threads (D) don't fix per-request CPU.
scenarios.hint: Width means 'often' — can the work be skipped instead of sped up?

scenarios.title: Cache Optimization: Row vs Column
scenarios.situation: A 4096x4096 matrix is stored row-major in a vector. A column-normalization pass iterates columns in the outer loop and rows in the inner loop. It runs 8x slower than the row pass, with perf showing high cache-miss rates and the CPU stalled on memory.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Buy faster RAM
Transpose the loop order (rows outer, columns inner) or transpose the data layout so the inner loop walks contiguous memory — sequential access prefetches; strided column access defeats it
Use a bigger L3 cache CPU
Parallelize the column loop across threads
scenarios.why: Row-major + column-outer traversal strides 16KB per access (4096 x 4 bytes), touching a new cache line every element and defeating the prefetcher — the classic cache-oblivious failure. Walking rows in the inner loop makes access sequential: one miss per 16 floats, then prefetch streams. Hardware (A/C) can't fix an algorithmic access pattern; threading (D) multiplies the memory traffic.
scenarios.hint: How many bytes apart are consecutive accesses in the inner loop?

scenarios.title: Allocation Reduction in the Parser
scenarios.situation: A log parser processes 500k lines/sec but spends 45% of CPU in malloc/free. Each line creates several std::strings and a vector of tokens. The strings are short-lived — used within one line's processing then discarded.
scenarios.prompt: What allocation strategy fits this short-lived pattern?
choices: Use a custom global new/delete override
Reuse buffers: string_views into the line buffer instead of owning strings, reserve() token vectors and clear() them per line, or use a per-line arena/bump allocator
Switch to a faster malloc implementation only
Process fewer lines per second
scenarios.why: Short-lived, same-size-ish allocations are the arena/bump-allocator sweet spot — or better, avoid owning allocations entirely with string_view into the input buffer and reused (reserved, cleared) containers. A faster malloc (C) helps marginally but the count is the problem; global new overrides (A) are a blunt instrument; throttling (D) surrenders throughput.
scenarios.hint: The allocations all die within microseconds — what allocation pattern matches that lifetime?

scenarios.title: Algorithm Choice Beats Micro-Tuning
scenarios.situation: A deduplication step does a linear scan over a 2M-element vector for each of 500k lookups — 30 minutes runtime. A teammate is hand-unrolling the scan loop with SIMD intrinsics, projecting a 4x speedup to ~7 minutes.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right call?
choices: Approve the SIMD work — 4x is a big win
Change the algorithm: sort + binary search or unordered_set turns O(n) lookups into O(log n)/O(1) — from 30 minutes to seconds, dwarfing the 4x micro-tune
Both: SIMD first, then the algorithm change
Buy a faster CPU
scenarios.why: Complexity class dominates constants: 500k x 2M linear scans is 10^12 comparisons; a hash set makes it ~500k operations — a 1000x+ win versus the 4x from SIMD heroics. Optimize the algorithm first, then micro-tune the new hot spot if needed. SIMD-first (A/C) polishes a fundamentally wrong approach; hardware (D) buys maybe 30%.
scenarios.hint: Compare 4x against the gap between O(n) and O(1) per lookup.
evidence: Replaces linear scan with hash set

scenarios.title: Branch Prediction: The Sorted Advantage
scenarios.situation: A filter loop `if (data[i] > threshold)` over 100M random floats takes 2.1s. Sorting the data first (0.4s) drops the filter to 0.5s — total 0.9s. The team is uneasy: 'sorting to make a branch faster feels like a hack.'
scenarios.prompt: Is the sort-then-filter legitimate, and why does it work?
choices: No — it's a hack; rewrite with branchless arithmetic instead

Yes, when reused: sorted data makes the branch perfectly predictable (all-false then all-true), eliminating mispredict penalties (~15-20 cycles each); it's legitimate if the sorted order is reused or the win exceeds sort cost
No — the CPU will learn the random pattern eventually
Yes, always sort before every loop
scenarios.why: Random data mispredicts ~50% of branches at ~15+ cycles each; sorted data predicts ~100% — the physics is real, not a hack. But it's only a win when the math works: sort cost amortized over reuse, or when order doesn't matter. Branchless (A) is the alternative when sorting isn't affordable; CPUs can't learn randomness (C); 'always sort' (D) ignores the cost side.
scenarios.hint: What does the branch predictor see in random data versus sorted data?
evidence: Explains predictability win with cost check

scenarios.title: Vectorization: Why Isn't It SIMD?
scenarios.situation: A simple loop `for (i) c[i] = a[i] + b[i];` over float arrays isn't auto-vectorized per the optimization report: 'loop not vectorized: possible dependence'. The arrays are raw pointers passed to the function.
scenarios.prompt: What blocks vectorization and what is the fix?
choices: The CPU doesn't support SIMD

Pointer aliasing: the compiler can't prove c doesn't overlap a/b, so it can't reorder; fix with __restrict__ (or -fno-strict-aliasing review / std::span with restrict semantics) to promise non-overlap
The loop is too simple for the vectorizer
Unroll the loop manually 8x
scenarios.why: The vectorizer must preserve semantics: if c aliases a, vectorized stores could clobber not-yet-loaded elements — so possible aliasing blocks it. __restrict__ (or restructuring to provably-separate spans) gives the compiler the non-overlap guarantee it needs. The CPU (A) surely supports SIMD for float adds; simplicity (C) is what vectorizers love; manual unrolling (D) doesn't resolve the dependence question.
scenarios.hint: What can't the compiler prove about three raw pointers?

scenarios.title: Inlining: The Call Overhead Mirage
scenarios.situation: Profiling shows 12% of time in a tiny 3-line accessor called 2B times. A developer marks it `inline` and sees no change — 'inline is broken'. The function is defined in a .cpp file; the callers are in other TUs.
scenarios.prompt: Why didn't inline help, and what actually fixes it?
choices: inline is just a hint; use __forceinline everywhere

inline doesn't cross TU boundaries at compile time without LTO: move the definition to the header (true inline availability) or enable link-time optimization (-flto) so the linker can inline across TUs
The profiler is wrong about the 12%
Make the accessor a macro
scenarios.why: `inline` is a linkage/ODR directive, not an inlining command — and crucially, a .cpp-defined function isn't visible to other TUs' optimizers at all, so no inlining decision is even possible there. Header definition makes the body available everywhere; LTO lets the linker optimize across TUs. __forceinline (A) can't inline what it can't see; macros (D) trade a build problem for a correctness problem.
scenarios.hint: Can the optimizer inline a function body it was never shown?
evidence: Moves definition to header or enables LTO

domains.name: Modern C++ (17/20/23)
domains.description: What 'modern' means in practice: the features interviewers expect you to know and use.

scenarios.title: Smart Pointer Selection: The Factory
scenarios.situation: A factory creates polymorphic `Renderer` objects. Some callers own the result exclusively; one registry needs shared ownership with weak observers. The current code returns raw pointers with a comment saying 'caller deletes'. Leaks are rampant.
scenarios.prompt: What ownership design fixes this?
choices: Return shared_ptr everywhere — sharing is safest
Return unique_ptr by default (explicit exclusive ownership, zero overhead); the registry converts to shared_ptr where genuinely shared, observers hold weak_ptr
Return raw pointers but document better
Return shared_ptr and never use weak_ptr
scenarios.why: unique_ptr is the default: it documents exclusive ownership at the type level and costs nothing. shared_ptr everywhere (A) pays atomic refcounting on every copy and invites cycles; observers must be weak_ptr or they keep objects alive. Raw pointers (C) are the status quo that leaks. The rule: unique by default, shared when shared, weak for non-owning observation.
scenarios.hint: Which ownership is the common case — and what should the default express?

scenarios.title: Move Semantics: The Return Trip
scenarios.situation: A function builds a 10MB `std::vector<Result>` and returns it. A reviewer insists on an out-parameter (`void fill(std::vector<Result>&)`) to 'avoid the copy'. The codebase is C++17.
scenarios.prompt: Is the out-parameter needed?
choices: Yes — returning large vectors always copies
No: NRVO/RVO elides the copy (guaranteed elision in C++17 for prvalues), and even without elision the move constructor transfers the buffer — the out-parameter is obsolete pessimization
Yes, but only for vectors over 1MB
Return a shared_ptr to the vector instead
scenarios.why: C++17 guarantees copy elision for prvalue returns, and named-return (NRVO) is near-universally applied; the fallback is a move, not a copy — the 10MB buffer is transferred, never duplicated. Out-parameters (A) pessimise readability for zero gain and defeat elision reasoning. Size thresholds (C) misunderstand moves; shared_ptr (D) adds refcounting to a value that has one owner.
scenarios.hint: What does the move constructor do to a vector's buffer — copy it or steal it?

scenarios.title: constexpr: Compile-Time Lookup Table
scenarios.situation: A CRC table of 256 entries is computed at startup on every process launch (~2ms) and in every unit test binary. The computation is pure: no I/O, no randomness. The table never changes.
scenarios.prompt: What is the modern C++ fix?
choices: Compute it once and hardcode the 256 numbers as literals
Make the generator constexpr and the table constinit/constexpr — computed at compile time, zero startup cost, and the compiler verifies the computation
Cache it in a file and load at startup
It's only 2ms — leave it
scenarios.why: constexpr moves pure computation to compile time: the table lands in the binary ready-made, startup cost vanishes, and the values stay derived from the algorithm (unlike hardcoded literals (A) which rot when the algorithm changes). File caching (C) adds I/O and deployment surface for a pure function; 'only 2ms' (D) ignores the multiplied cost across every test binary and process.
scenarios.hint: The computation is pure and the result is constant — when must it run?
objectives: Shift pure computation to compile time

scenarios.title: Concepts vs SFINAE: The Constrained Template
scenarios.situation: A template `process(T)` must only accept arithmetic types. The legacy code uses `std::enable_if_t<std::is_arithmetic_v<T>>` in the return type. New hires can't read it, and misuse produces 200-line substitution errors. The codebase is C++20.
scenarios.prompt: What is the modern replacement?
choices: Keep SFINAE — it works and everyone's used to it
Concepts: `template<std::integral T>` or a requires-clause — constraints are readable, checked at the declaration, and misuse yields a one-line 'constraints not satisfied' error
static_assert inside the function body
Overload for every arithmetic type manually
scenarios.why: Concepts check constraints at the point of declaration with clear diagnostics, versus SFINAE's substitution-failure novels buried in overload resolution. Readability for new hires is a real maintenance win. static_assert (C) fires later with worse overload behavior (no SFINAE-friendly exclusion); manual overloads (D) explode combinatorially; 'works' (A) ignores the diagnostic and readability cost.
scenarios.hint: Where should the constraint be checked — deep in substitution, or at the declaration?

scenarios.title: Ranges: The Pipeline Rewrite
scenarios.situation: A data-prep step chains: filter nulls, transform to scores, take top 100, then sort. The current code uses three temporary vectors and four loops. It's correct but allocates heavily and the intermediate steps are hard to follow.
scenarios.prompt: How do ranges improve this?
choices: Ranges are just syntax sugar; keep the loops
Compose a lazy view pipeline: `data | filter(...) | transform(...) | take(100)` then sort — no intermediate vectors, single readable expression of intent
Rewrite with raw for loops but fewer temporaries
Use ranges but materialize each stage for debuggability
scenarios.why: Views are lazy: the pipeline fuses into essentially one pass with no intermediate allocations, and the composed expression reads as the algorithm itself (filter->transform->take) instead of four loops shuffling temporaries. Materializing stages (D) keeps the allocation cost; raw loops (C) keep the readability cost; dismissing ranges (A) leaves both costs on the table.
scenarios.hint: What if the intermediate vectors never had to exist?

scenarios.title: Coroutines: The Async Read Chain
scenarios.situation: A network service chains 5 async reads with callbacks; error handling is scattered across lambdas and the 'flow' is unreadable. The team considers coroutines (C++20) but worries about 'hidden allocations and magic'.
scenarios.prompt: When are coroutines the right call here?
choices: Never — callbacks are explicit and coroutines hide control flow

Yes: `co_await` linearizes the chain into straight-line code with normal try/catch error handling; the 'magic' is a well-defined state machine, and allocation concerns are addressed by custom promise allocators / elision
Only if the team rewrites everything in async style first
Use threads instead — simpler mental model
scenarios.why: Coroutines turn callback spaghetti into sequential-looking code where errors propagate via exceptions normally — the readability win is exactly for multi-step async chains. The state machine is compiler-generated but deterministic, not magic; frame allocations can be customized away. Threads (D) trade a readability problem for a concurrency problem; 'never' (A) keeps the scattered error handling that's already hurting.
scenarios.hint: What does the error-handling code look like in each style?

scenarios.title: RAII: The Lock That Leaks
scenarios.situation: A function does `mutex.lock(); ...; if (error) return; ...; mutex.unlock();` A new early-return was added last week and production shows the mutex permanently held after certain errors — the service wedges. The team proposes 'be careful with returns'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the durable fix?
choices: Audit every return path and add unlock() calls
RAII: std::lock_guard / std::scoped_lock — the destructor unlocks on every exit path including exceptions; manual lock/unlock is the bug class itself
Ban early returns in locked regions
Use a recursive mutex so double-lock is safe
scenarios.why: Manual lock/unlock makes every future edit a potential deadlock — the bug class is 'unpaired unlock on some path', which code review cannot reliably prevent. RAII ties the unlock to scope exit: correct on all paths, including exceptions, by construction. Auditing (A) and banning returns (C) fight human fallibility with policy; recursive mutexes (D) mask rather than fix pairing bugs.
scenarios.hint: Which construct makes the wrong code unrepresentable instead of merely discouraged?

scenarios.title: string_view: The Substring That Dangles
scenarios.situation: A parser returns `std::string_view` into a temporary: `std::string_view get() { std::string s = build(); return std::string_view(s); }` Tests pass (the memory isn't reused yet in small tests); production crashes intermittently.
scenarios.prompt: What is the bug and the rule?
choices: string_view is unsafe and should never be used

The view dangles: the temporary string dies at return, leaving a view of freed memory — string_view is non-owning, so never return it pointing at locals/temporaries; return std::string (moved) or ensure the viewed data outlives the view
Tests should use bigger inputs
Make the local static
scenarios.why: string_view is a non-owning (pointer, length) pair — returning one over a destroyed local is use-after-free that small tests mask (freed memory often still mapped). The rule: a view must never outlive its viewed data. Return an owning std::string (moves are cheap) or view into longer-lived storage. Banning string_view (A) discards its real value for parameters; static locals (D) introduce thread-safety and lifetime puzzles.
scenarios.hint: Who owns the characters the view points at after the return?

lessons.title: Core Syntax — Core concepts
concepts: auto deduction: use const auto& when only reading, to avoid copies of expensive types.
Most vexing parse: C++ grammar prefers to parse Widget w(); as a function declaration (returning Widget, taking no parameters) rather than a variable definition.

Uniform initialization: list initialization (braces) makes narrowing conversions — those that can lose information, like double→int — ill-formed. Brace initialization Widget w{} unambiguously defines an object — and additionally forbids narrowing conversions.
List initialization: parenthesized and = initialization permit them silently.

example.code:
using namespace std;  // in a header: affects every includer
// ... later, someone's `count` collides with std::count
example.walkthrough: A using-directive in a header is transitive: everyone who includes it (directly or indirectly) gets the entire namespace injected, inviting collisions like a local count vs std::count and silently changing overload resolution. Keep using-directives in .cpp files after all includes, or qualify with std::.

pitfalls: Common trap: const references cannot call any member functions.
Common trap: uniform initialization only works for aggregates.
Common trap: auto cannot deduce numeric types in loops.
Common trap: the first declared overload always wins ties.

lessons.title: OOP in C++ — Core concepts
concepts: Virtual destructors: = 0 declares a pure virtual function with no required implementation in the base, making the class abstract — it can be used as a pointer/reference type but never instantiated.
Polymorphic deletion: rule: any class designed as a base with polymorphic use needs a virtual destructor — often virtual ~Base() = default.

Object slicing: copying a derived object into a base-typed variable slices off everything beyond the base subobject, including the dynamic type — virtual calls then resolve to Base. While the base constructor runs, the derived members have not been constructed — the object's dynamic type is effectively the base.
Passing by (const) reference or pointer keeps the complete object and its dynamic type intact. The fix: pass needed data as constructor parameters, or use a post-construction init step.
override specifier: the override specifier makes the compiler verify the override — a signature mismatch becomes an error at the declaration, not a silent runtime surprise.

example.code:
void process(Base b) { b.speak(); }  // takes Base BY VALUE
Derived d; process(d);  // d sliced to its Base subobject; speak() is Base's
example.walkthrough: Copying a derived object into a base-typed variable slices off everything beyond the base subobject, including the dynamic type — virtual calls then resolve to Base. Slicing is silent and compiles without warnings.

pitfalls: Common trap: setup() must be pure virtual for dispatch to work in constructors.
Common trap: virtual functions cannot be redeclared in derived classes.
Common trap: the access specifier only affects data members, not functions.
Common trap: the base pointer must be cast to Derived* for virtual dispatch.

lessons.title: STL Containers — Core concepts
concepts: Iterator invalidation: algorithms operate on iterator ranges, not containers — std::remove cannot change v's size, so it compacts the kept elements to the front and returns the new logical end.
vector reallocation: a vector stores elements contiguously; when push_back exceeds capacity it allocates a bigger buffer and moves everything, leaving old iterators dangling.

Map::operator[] is specified to insert a value-initialized element when the key is absent — convenient for counting, surprising for lookups. Ordered map needs only operator<; unordered_map needs a hash (to pick a bucket) and equality (to resolve collisions).
find vs at: for read-only access use find() (returns end() if missing) or at() (throws out_of_range).
Erase-remove idiom: the erase-remove idiom, v.erase(std::remove(...), v.end()), erases the leftover tail.

example.code:
std::remove(v.begin(), v.end(), expired);  // elements shifted, size unchanged!
// v.erase(std::remove(...), v.end()); is the full idiom
example.walkthrough: Algorithms operate on iterator ranges, not containers — std::remove cannot change v's size, so it compacts the kept elements to the front and returns the new logical end. (C++20's std::erase(v, value) does both in one call.).

pitfalls: Common trap: operator[] throws std::out_of_range on missing keys.
Common trap: a vector iterator cannot be dereferenced twice.
Common trap: std::sort requires a total order.
Common trap: std::remove requires a sorted range.

lessons.title: Memory & Smart Pointers — Core concepts
concepts: Exception safety: RAII ties resource release to object lifetime: the lock_guard's destructor runs when the scope exits for any reason — return, exception, or fall-through — so the mutex cannot be left locked.

unique_ptr: the compiler may evaluate new Widget, then priority(), then the unique_ptr constructor — if priority() throws in between, the raw pointer is lost and leaks. std::make_unique performs the allocation directly into the smart pointer's control path, eliminating the window.
Move semantics: std::move is a cast to an rvalue reference; the move constructor then steals the source's resources. (unique_lock adds deferred/try semantics when needed.).

Shared_ptr destroys its object when the last owner goes away, but in a cycle every object has an owner inside the cycle — the count never drops to zero. weak_ptr holds a non-owning reference: it can lock() to a temporary shared_ptr when access is needed, and it does not keep the target alive.

example.code:
take(std::unique_ptr<Widget>(new Widget), priority());
// if priority() throws after new but before the unique_ptr is built: leak
example.walkthrough: The compiler may evaluate new Widget, then priority(), then the unique_ptr constructor — if priority() throws in between, the raw pointer is lost and leaks. std::make_unique performs the allocation directly into the smart pointer's control path, eliminating the window. It is also shorter and exception-safe by construction. (make_shared additionally fuses the object and control block into one allocation.).

pitfalls: Common trap: std::move destroys the source.
Common trap: wrap the call in try/catch and delete manually in the catch block.
Common trap: scalar delete works for arrays of trivial types.
Common trap: delete on arrays leaks the count prefix.

lessons.title: Templates & Lambdas — Core concepts
concepts: Template argument deduction works from the argument types regardless of whether the parameter is T, T&, or T const& — the parameter form only controls how the argument binds. Fix it by header-only definitions; explicit instantiation (template int twice<int>(int);) works when the type set is closed and known.
Reference parameters: a reference capture stores a reference to the local variable, not its value — it dangles exactly like a returned pointer to a local.

Lambda captures: since C++14, auto in a lambda parameter list makes the call operator a function template; each distinct argument type triggers an instantiation. By-reference capture is safe only when the lambda is used within the captured variables' lifetime (e.g., passed to std::sort).
Constexpr permits a function to be evaluated at compile time when called with constant expressions, and requires it to be usable there.

example.code:
template <typename T>
T const& max(T const& a, T const& b) { return a < b ? b : a; }  // references: no copies
example.walkthrough: Template argument deduction works from the argument types regardless of whether the parameter is T, T&, or T const& — the parameter form only controls how the argument binds. T const& binds without copying and accepts temporaries, which is why the standard library's generic algorithms take their arguments this way.

pitfalls: Common trap: compile-time computation requires template metaprogramming.
Common trap: generic lambdas require C++20 concepts.
Common trap: templates cannot deduce reference types.
Common trap: concepts make templates run faster.

lessons.title: Build & Toolchain — Core concepts
concepts: Key function: the compiler emits a class's vtable in the translation unit containing the definition of its first non-inline virtual function (the 'key function').

One Definition Rule: modern CMake is target-based: target_include_directories (and target_link_libraries, target_compile_features) attach usage requirements to one target, with PRIVATE (build only), PUBLIC (build + consumers), and INTERFACE (consumers only) controlling propagation precisely.
Principle: if that function is declared but never defined — commonly a forgotten virtual destructor — no TU emits the vtable and the link fails.

example.code:
clang++ -std=c++20 -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g -o tests *.cpp
./tests  # aborts with symbolicated trace on first error
example.walkthrough: AddressSanitizer instruments memory accesses to catch heap/stack/global overflows, use-after-free, and leaks (with LeakSanitizer); UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer catches signed-integer overflow, bad shifts, misaligned access, and null dereference. Together at ~2x slowdown they are the highest-signal automated memory check available — far beyond what warnings alone can prove.

pitfalls: Common trap: set the include path as an environment variable instead of in CMake.
Common trap: static libraries cannot satisfy references from .cpp files.
Common trap: merge all targets into one executable so the leak does not matter.
Common trap: linkers cannot handle virtual functions.

lessons.title: C++ — Core concepts
concepts: RAII ties resource lifetime to object lifetime: acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor. Stack-allocated objects clean themselves up on every exit path — including exceptions — which is why manual new/delete is rare in modern code.

Smart pointers encode ownership: unique_ptr for exclusive ownership (movable, never copied — use std::make_unique), shared_ptr for shared ownership via reference counting (use std::make_shared), and weak_ptr for non-owning back-references that break cycles.

Move semantics transfer resources instead of copying them: an rvalue reference (T&&) parameter can steal the source's heap buffer and leave it in a valid-but-empty state. This makes returning large objects by value cheap and powers efficient standard containers.

The STL gives you containers (vector, map/unordered_map, set), iterators (the glue between containers and algorithms), and algorithms (<algorithm>: sort, find_if, transform). Prefer algorithms over hand loops — they state intent and get the edge cases right.

Templates are compile-time code generation: function and class templates are instantiated per type used, giving zero-overhead genericity. Templates are duck-typed at instantiation — errors surface where used, which is why concepts (C++20) exist to constrain them up front.

Value semantics by default: C++ copies unless you say otherwise (references, std::move). The rule of zero (let the compiler generate special members when members manage themselves), three, and five governs when you must write copy/move operations and destructors yourself.

example.walkthrough: make_unique creates the vector with exclusive ownership — no raw new, no leak if push_back throws. Returning *names moves the vector's heap buffer into the caller's vector (no string copies), and the emptied unique_ptr's destructor safely deletes nothing.

pitfalls: Common trap: shared_ptr cycles — back-pointers must be weak_ptr or objects never die.
Common trap: using a moved-from object as if it still held its value — it is valid but unspecified; reassign before use.
Common trap: erasing from a container while iterating without using erase's return value — iterator invalidation.
Common trap: `std::move` doesn't move anything by itself — it just casts to an rvalue; the move constructor does the work.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it: Start Here first, then work each domain in listed order. Domains unlock as you demonstrate mastery, because C++ Technical Interview topics build on each other.
What 'terminal' means: the Terminal tab is a real shell where labs run. Every lab command executes there — you learn by doing, not by reading about doing.
Lessons teach concepts with a worked example, pitfalls, and a try-it prompt. Scenarios test judgment under realistic pressure. Labs prove you can execute. The mock assessment ties it all together.
Knowledge checks verify understanding before a lesson counts complete — you cannot click through. Spaced repetition resurfaces weak areas automatically.
Your progress syncs as you work. A domain is mastered when lessons are verified, scenarios answered, and labs completed.

example.code:
Day 1: complete all 4 Start Here lessons
Day 2-3: first two content domains (lessons + scenarios)
Day 4+: one domain per day, labs each evening
Final 3 days: mock assessment runs + capstone build
example.walkthrough: This order exists because later domains assume earlier vocabulary. Skipping ahead creates gaps that the mock assessment will expose — painfully. Trust the sequence.

pitfalls: Skimming lessons without attempting the knowledge check — verification is the learning, not a gate to dodge.
Doing scenarios before reading the domain lessons — scenarios assume the concepts; you will guess instead of reason.
Ignoring the Terminal labs — hands-on execution is what separates passing from failing on performance-based questions.

lessons.title: C++ Technical Interview Exam Strategy
concepts: C++ Technical Interview tests applied judgment more than memorization. Roughly a third of questions are scenario-based: read the situation, eliminate distractors, pick the BEST answer — not merely a correct one.
Performance-based questions (PBQs) simulate real tasks: drag-and-drop, CLI output analysis, log reading. The labs in this bootcamp are PBQ rehearsal — treat every lab as exam practice.
Time budget: divide total minutes by question count before you start, then check the clock every 20 questions. Flag hard questions and move on — a stuck minute is a lost minute.
Elimination first: cross out the two obviously wrong choices, then compare the remaining two against the question's constraints (cheapest? most secure? first step?).
Never leave a question blank. There is no penalty for wrong answers — an educated guess beats an empty one every time.

example.code:
Q: 'A user reports... Which should you do FIRST?'
  → The word FIRST is the whole question.
  → Eliminate any choice that is a later step.
  → Among the rest, pick the diagnostic before the fix.
example.walkthrough: Exam writers love FIRST, BEST, MOST, and LEAST. Those words change the answer even when the scenario looks identical. Read the actual question stem twice — once for the story, once for the ask.

pitfalls: Answering the scenario instead of the question — the story is context; the final sentence is the task.
Changing answers on review without new evidence — first instincts outperform second-guessing statistically.
Memorizing acronyms without understanding the process behind them — PBQs punish surface knowledge.

lessons.title: Study System: Spaced Repetition That Sticks
concepts: Forgetting is the default — plan for it. Review a domain's key concepts at expanding intervals: 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 14 days. Each successful recall strengthens the memory trace.
Active recall beats re-reading: close the lesson and explain the concept aloud in your own words. If you cannot explain it, you do not know it yet.
Interleave domains instead of block-studying one: mix scenarios from two domains in a session. Exams mix topics — your practice should too.
The Feynman check: after each lesson, write a 3-sentence explanation a junior could follow. Vague sentences reveal vague understanding.
Weekly rhythm: 2 domains + daily coding problems; mock interviews at week 4 and 6.

example.code:
Session template (90 min):
  0-10   warm-up: 5 flashcards / quick recalls
  10-50  new domain: lessons + knowledge checks
  50-75  scenarios from today + one older domain (interleaving)
  75-90  one terminal lab, then 3-sentence Feynman writes
example.walkthrough: Ninety focused minutes beat four distracted hours. The template above is engineered for retention, not seat time — protect the lab block, it is where skills become reflexes.

pitfalls: Re-reading notes and calling it studying — recognition is not recall; the exam tests recall.
Cramming new domains the night before — sleep consolidates memory; an all-nighter trades retention for exhaustion.
Skipping the Feynman write — it feels slow, but it is the fastest diagnostic of real understanding.

lessons.title: Systems Thinking: Your Unfair Advantage
concepts: Exams and interviews reward systems thinkers: people who trace a request end-to-end instead of reciting isolated facts. This bootcamp trains that explicitly in the Systems Anatomy domain.
The four-step method: (1) see the whole in context, (2) cut it open to reveal layers, (3) walk the process step-by-step, (4) pull apart into labeled pieces.
Every troubleshooting scenario here is a systems trace in disguise: start from the symptom, walk backward through dependencies, find where the expected flow diverges from reality.
In interviews, narrate the journey: 'the request starts here, then…' — hiring managers hear senior-level thinking when you trace instead of define.

Strong answer: 'The stub resolver asks the recursive resolver, which walks root → TLD → authoritative, caching at each level — that is why the first lookup is slow and the second is instant.'
