lessons.title: Mock Assessment Briefing: Rules of Engagement
concepts: The mock simulates C++ Technical Interview conditions: timed, mixed-domain, no hints, one shot per question. Treat it as the real exam — same chair, same focus, no phone.
Scoring mirrors the real exam's weighting: scenario judgment counts more than recall. A wrong answer on a multi-step scenario costs more than a missed definition.
Run the mock only after all domains show 80%+ mastery. Running it early wastes its diagnostic value — it is a measuring instrument, not a study tool.
After each run, the review breaks down misses by domain. Your next study block targets exactly those domains — the mock tells you where to aim.
Two full runs minimum: the first finds gaps, the second confirms they are closed. A passing second run is your green light.

example.code:
Mock protocol:
  1. Silence notifications, full-screen the bootcamp
  2. Note start time; budget per-question time on paper
  3. Answer every question — no blanks
  4. Flag-and-move on stuck questions; return with fresh eyes
  5. Review the domain breakdown before any celebration
example.walkthrough: The mock's value is the breakdown, not the score. A 68% with a clear miss-map beats a lucky 82% — the map tells you exactly what to study next.

pitfalls: Peeking at notes mid-mock — it inflates the score and destroys the diagnostic.
Running the mock as a first activity — without domain mastery it only measures unpreparedness.
Ignoring the domain breakdown — the score is trivia; the miss-map is the study plan.
lessons.try_it: Check your domain mastery percentages now. List any domain under 80% — those are your pre-mock targets.

lessons.title: Reviewing a Mock Run: Turning Misses into Mastery
concepts: For every missed question, classify the error: knowledge gap (never learned it), application gap (knew it, misapplied it), or reading error (misread the ask). Each type needs a different fix.
Knowledge gaps go back to the domain lesson — re-read, re-verify, Feynman-write. Application gaps need more scenarios, not more reading. Reading errors need the exam-strategy lesson again.
Keep an error log: question topic, error type, correct reasoning in one sentence. Patterns emerge fast — three 'reading errors' in a row is a process problem, not a knowledge problem.
Re-test missed topics within 48 hours with fresh scenarios. A corrected mistake that is not re-tested is a mistake waiting to recur.
Your second mock run should show misses migrating: fewer knowledge gaps, zero repeated reading errors. That migration is the signal you are ready.

example.code:
Error log entry:
  Q: firewall rule order scenario → chose 'deny' before 'allow'
  Type: application gap (knew rule order, misapplied under time pressure)
  Fix: 5 more firewall scenarios, timed
  Correct reasoning: 'First match wins — the allow had to precede the deny.'
example.walkthrough: Do not just re-read the explanation and move on. The error log forces you to name the failure mode — and named failures are fixable failures.

pitfalls: Re-reading explanations passively — recognition feels like learning but evaporates under pressure.
Studying only the missed topics and neglecting maintenance review of strong ones — strengths decay too.
Taking the second mock too soon — give fixes 48 hours and a re-test cycle first.
lessons.try_it: Create your error log file now (paper or notes app). You will need it after your first mock run.

lessons.title: Capstone Plan: What You Will Build and Why
concepts: Employers and examiners trust demonstrated skill over claimed knowledge. Your capstone is a working artifact — something you can screenshare and narrate in under 10 minutes.
Pick ONE project from the list below. Depth beats breadth: a single polished build outperforms three half-finished ones.
Scope it to finish in 2–3 focused sessions. If it needs more, cut features — a complete small project beats an ambitious pile of parts.
Document as you go: every decision gets a one-line reason. That log becomes your interview narration script.
Done means: it works end-to-end, you can demo it live, and you can explain every part without notes.

example.code:
Pick your project:
  1. Custom Container Library — a tested vector/map implementation with benchmarks
  2. Multithreaded Server — a thread-pool TCP server with clean shutdown
  3. Game Engine Subsystem — an ECS or renderer with modern C++ throughout
example.walkthrough: Choose the project that scares you slightly — that is where the growth is. But cap the scope ruthlessly: you must finish.

pitfalls: Starting two projects and finishing neither — pick one, finish it, then consider a second.
Building without documenting — the demo narration is half the value; no log means no story.
Gold-plating instead of finishing — ship the working core first, polish only if time remains.
lessons.try_it: Write your one-paragraph project selection rationale now: which project, why it fits your goals, and what 'done' looks like.

lessons.title: Build Log: Decisions, Dead Ends, and Proof
concepts: Keep a build log with timestamps: what you tried, what happened, what you changed. Dead ends are valuable — they prove you debugged, not just followed a tutorial.
For each component, record: purpose (one line), how it works (three lines), how you tested it (one command or check).
Screenshot or record key milestones. A 60-second screen recording of the working project is worth more than a page of description.
Version your work: even a simple dated folder structure beats a single 'final' file. Show the progression.
The log is not overhead — it IS the deliverable's companion. Interviewers ask 'tell me about a challenge'; your log hands you the answer.

example.code:
Build log entry:
  14:32 — Tried X config; service failed with error Y
  14:47 — Found cause: Z was misconfigured (docs said A, reality was B)
  15:05 — Fixed; verified with [test command]; works end-to-end
example.walkthrough: Write the log as you go, not after. Memory lies; timestamps do not. Future-you (in the interview) will thank present-you.

pitfalls: Writing the log from memory at the end — you will forget the dead ends, which are the best stories.
Skipping the 'how I tested it' line — untested claims collapse under the first interview question.
No recordings — a live demo can fail; a recording is bulletproof backup.
lessons.try_it: Create your build log file now with today's date and your project title as the header.

lessons.title: Demo Day: Narrating Your Build in 10 Minutes
concepts: Structure the demo: problem (1 min) → architecture (2 min) → live walkthrough (5 min) → lessons learned (2 min). Rehearse it twice, timed.
Narrate the systems journey: 'a request starts here, flows through…' — the Systems Anatomy voice. Show you understand the whole, not just the parts you typed.
Prepare for three hard questions: 'why this approach over X?', 'what breaks at scale?', 'what would you do differently?'. Write your answers in advance.
Lead with the working demo, not slides. Working software presented live beats any deck.
End with the repo/README link and offer to walk through the code. Make it effortless for them to verify your work.

example.code:
Demo script skeleton:
  'I built [X] because [problem]. It works by [3-step journey].
   Watch: [live action]. The tricky part was [challenge] —
   I solved it by [approach]. Code and docs are at [link].'
example.walkthrough: Rehearsal is non-negotiable. A polished 10-minute demo signals preparation, communication skill, and genuine ownership — exactly what hiring managers screen for.

pitfalls: Wing the demo — 'let me just show you' without a plan wastes the moment.
Hiding the challenges — the dead ends and fixes are what prove real engineering happened.
No backup plan — have the recording ready in case live demo gods are unkind.
lessons.try_it: Draft your three hard-question answers now, before you build. They will sharpen your design decisions.

lessons.title: Roles That Hire C++ Programming Skills
concepts: The roles: C++ Developer, Systems Programmer, Game Engine Developer, HFT Developer. Read 10 job postings and extract the repeated requirements — that list is your real syllabus.
Titles vary by company; skills cluster by function. Map postings to skill clusters (not titles) to see what the market actually buys.
Entry points differ: some roles hire on certification + projects, others on portfolio + interviews. Know your target's gate before optimizing for it.
Salary bands follow scarcity + impact: specialized + revenue-adjacent pays more. Position yourself at that intersection deliberately.
Track the market quarterly: which skills are rising in postings? Your learning backlog should follow the demand signal.

example.code:
Posting analysis template:
  Role: ___
  Repeated requirements (3+ postings): ___
  Nice-to-haves: ___
  My gaps: ___ → study priority
example.walkthrough: The job posting is the employer's requirements doc. Analyze it like one — systematically, not hopefully.

pitfalls: Chasing titles instead of skill clusters — the same skills hide under five different titles.
Ignoring the 'repeated requirements' — what 8/10 postings demand is the real bar.
No gap analysis — studying without knowing your gaps is motion without direction.
lessons.try_it: Pull 5 postings for your target role now. List the top 5 repeated requirements.

lessons.title: Resume & Projects That Get Callbacks
concepts: Resumes get 30 seconds: lead with a skills line matching the posting's keywords, then 3-4 bullets per role with quantified outcomes (not duties).
Projects beat buzzwords: one deployed, documented project outweighs a paragraph of claimed skills. Link the repo AND the live demo.
Tailor per application: mirror the posting's language for the top 5 requirements. ATS filters are literal — 'PostgreSQL' does not match 'postgres' in dumb parsers.
The capstone in this bootcamp IS your resume project: finish it, document it, link it. That single line does more work than any certification bullet.
GitHub profile hygiene: pinned repos with READMEs, green contribution squares, no empty forks. Recruiters do click through.

example.code:
Bullet formula: [Action verb] + [what] + [scale] + [outcome]
  Weak: 'Responsible for databases.'
  Strong: 'Migrated 2TB analytics DB to Postgres; cut query p95 40%; zero-downtime cutover.'
example.walkthrough: Every bullet must answer: what did you do, at what scale, to what effect? Duties describe jobs; outcomes get interviews.

pitfalls: Skill lists without evidence — every claimed skill needs a project or role bullet backing it.
One generic resume for all applications — tailoring is the highest-ROI 20 minutes in job hunting.
No links — a project without a URL might as well not exist.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite your weakest resume bullet using the formula above. Quantify something.

lessons.title: Interview Loops: What Actually Happens
concepts: Typical loop: recruiter screen (15 min, fit + comp) → technical screen (45-60 min, live problems) → onsite/virtual loop (3-5 rounds: technical depth, system design, behavioral) → offer.
Technical screens test thinking aloud: narrate your approach before coding/querying. Silence is scored as stuck; structured thinking is scored as senior.
Behavioral rounds use STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) — prepare 5 stories covering: conflict, failure, leadership, ambiguity, and impact. Quantify results.
Questions YOU ask matter: 'what does success look like in 90 days?' and 'what's the hardest problem the team faces?' signal seriousness. Never ask nothing.
Follow up within 24 hours: thank-you note referencing something specific from the conversation. Small effort, real signal.

example.code:
STAR story skeleton:
  S: 'Our deploy pipeline broke weekly...'
  T: 'I owned stabilizing it in Q3...'
  A: 'I added staged rollouts + runbook...'
  R: 'Deploys went from 60% to 99% success; on-call pages dropped 70%.'
example.walkthrough: Prepare stories, not scripts: know your 5 STAR stories cold enough to adapt to any behavioral question. Rehearse aloud twice.

pitfalls: No questions for them — reads as disinterest; always ask two.
Rambling technical answers — structure: approach first, then detail, then verify.
Badmouthing past employers — the interviewer hears how you will talk about THEM.
lessons.try_it: Draft one STAR story now using the skeleton. Time it — aim for 90 seconds.

lessons.title: The C++ Programming Tool Landscape
concepts: Tools cluster by job-to-be-done, not by vendor. Learn the categories first, then pick one tool per category deeply — depth in one beats surface in five.
The 80/20 rule: 20% of each tool's features cover 80% of real work. Master the core workflow before exploring the edges.
Free/open tiers are enough to learn: every major platform has a free tier or community edition sufficient for portfolio projects. Never pay to learn the basics.
Tool churn is constant; fundamentals are stable. SQL outlives every BI tool; TCP/IP outlives every cloud console. Invest in fundamentals first.

For C++ Programming, the essential categories:
  Compiler: GCC/Clang
  Build: CMake
  Debugger: GDB/LLDB
  Sanitizers: ASan/TSan/UBSan

example.code:
Learning order:
  1. One tool per category, core workflow only
  2. Build the capstone using exactly these tools
  3. Add a second tool per category only when a job posting demands it
example.walkthrough: Resist tool tourism: each new tool costs weeks. The portfolio proves depth; the resume lists breadth honestly.

pitfalls: Learning 5 tools shallowly instead of 2 deeply — interviews probe depth.
Paying for premium tiers to learn — free tiers cover 90% of learning needs.
Chasing every new release — fundamentals first; novelty second.
lessons.try_it: List your one-tool-per-category stack now. Identify any category where you have zero depth — that is your next lab.

lessons.title: Workflows: Connecting the Tools
concepts: Tools in isolation are trivia; workflows are skill. The professional unit is the end-to-end flow: ingest → transform → validate → deliver — across YOUR tool stack.
Document your workflows as runbooks: trigger, steps, verification, rollback. A runbook turns personal knowledge into team capability.
Automate the toil, not the judgment: repetitive steps get scripted; decisions stay human. If you do it weekly, automate it.
Version everything: code, configs, queries, dashboards. 'Final_v2_ACTUAL' is not version control — git is.
The workflow IS the portfolio piece: 'here is my pipeline, here is the runbook, here is the monitoring' — that sentence hires.

example.code:
Runbook skeleton:
  Trigger: ___ (schedule/event/manual)
  Steps: 1.___ 2.___ 3.___
  Verify: ___ (how do you know it worked?)
  Rollback: ___ (how do you undo it?)
  Owner: ___  Last tested: ___
example.walkthrough: Write the runbook BEFORE automating: it forces you to understand the workflow well enough to hand it to someone else.

pitfalls: Automating before documenting — you encode confusion at machine speed.
No verification step — a workflow without a check is a hope with extra steps.
No rollback plan — the first failure without one teaches this lesson permanently.
lessons.try_it: Write a runbook for one workflow you do regularly, using the skeleton above.

lessons.title: Ownership: The Interview's Favorite Topic
concepts: Every C++ interview probes ownership: who creates, who destroys, who can copy, who can move. Answer with smart pointers by default and raw pointers only for non-owning observation.
unique_ptr = exclusive ownership, move-only. shared_ptr = shared ownership, reference-counted, cyclic danger. weak_ptr = non-owning observer that breaks cycles. Know which to reach for and why.
Rule of 0/3/5: if you define none of destructor/copy/move, the compiler does it right (Rule of 0 — prefer). If you define a destructor, you probably need copy+move too (Rule of 5).
'What does this print' traps hinge on lifetimes: dangling references, use-after-move, static init order. Trace object lifetimes line by line — the answer is always in the lifetime.
Move semantics: moved-from objects are valid-but-unspecified. Never use a moved-from object except to reassign or destroy it. Interviewers love this edge.

example.walkthrough: Ownership questions have one right framing: 'who owns this memory, and how is that expressed in the type system?' Answer in those terms every time.

pitfalls: Returning raw owning pointers from factories — the caller cannot know they must delete; return unique_ptr.
shared_ptr by default — cycles and atomic refcount cost; default to unique_ptr, upgrade deliberately.
Using moved-from objects — valid-but-unspecified means the only safe operations are destruction and reassignment.
lessons.try_it: Write the Rule of 5 declarations for a class owning a raw buffer, then rewrite it with unique_ptr (Rule of 0). Compare.

lessons.title: The Memory Model in Plain Terms
concepts: Threads share memory; the memory model defines what 'share' guarantees. Without synchronization, concurrent access to the same non-atomic variable is a data race — undefined behavior, not 'probably fine'.
Mutexes give mutual exclusion: lock, touch shared state, unlock. Keep critical sections tiny — the lock is a serialization point, and serialization kills scaling.
Atomics (std::atomic) give lock-free operations on single variables with memory-ordering guarantees. Default to seq_cst; reach for relaxed/acquire-release only with a written justification.
Deadlock needs four conditions (Coffman): mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait. Break any one — lock ordering (always acquire in the same global order) breaks circular wait.
Prefer higher-level tools: std::jthread (joins automatically), std::latch/barrier, thread pools over raw threads. Raw thread + manual join is where leaks and races breed.

example.walkthrough: Reason about concurrency in terms of shared state and its protection. Every shared variable needs a named guardian: a mutex, an atomic, or documented immutability.

pitfalls: Locking at the wrong granularity — one giant lock serializes everything; per-object locks risk deadlock without ordering.
Double-checked locking without atomics/fences — the classic broken pattern; use call_once or magic statics.
Detached threads accessing locals — the stack frame dies; the thread must not outlive what it touches.
lessons.try_it: Implement a thread-safe counter three ways: mutex, atomic, sharded. Benchmark and explain the scaling difference.

lessons.title: Profiling Before Optimizing
concepts: Measure first: perf, Tracy, or even chrono timers around suspects. The hotspot is never where you guess — profile data beats intuition 9 times out of 10.
Big-O dominates micro-optimization: an O(n²) algorithm with bit-twiddling still loses to O(n log n). Fix complexity before touching the inner loop.
Cache is king: sequential access patterns, struct-of-arrays for hot loops, and avoiding pointer chasing. A cache miss costs ~100ns; an L1 hit costs ~1ns — layout IS performance.
Allocation is expensive: reuse buffers, prefer stack, use object pools for hot paths. Profile allocations (heaptrack) before assuming the algorithm is slow.
Compiler flags matter: -O2/-O3, link-time optimization, PGO. Measure with the same flags as production — debug builds lie about performance.

example.code:
Slow: for (auto* p : ptrs) sum += p->value;  // pointer chase, cache misses
Faster: struct { float* values; } soa; for (i) sum += soa.values[i]; // sequential
Measure: perf stat shows cache-misses dropping 10x; wall time follows.
example.walkthrough: Optimization without profiling is astrology. The workflow is sacred: profile → hypothesize → change ONE thing → measure → keep or revert.

pitfalls: Optimizing without measuring — the #1 performance sin; you will 'fix' the wrong thing.
Micro-optimizing an O(n²) algorithm — complexity first, always.
Benchmarking debug builds — meaningless numbers; optimize what ships.
lessons.try_it: Profile any program you have with `perf stat`. Identify the top hotspot and state whether it is CPU, cache, or allocation-bound.

lessons.title: C++20 Features Interviewers Expect
concepts: Concepts: constrain templates with named requirements (std::integral, std::ranges::range). Replaces SFINAE puzzles with readable errors — use them on every new template.
Ranges: composable lazy views (filter | transform) over sequences. Prefer ranges to raw loops for expressiveness — but know when a plain loop is clearer.
Coroutines: async code without callbacks. Know the vocabulary (promise, awaitable) even if you have not shipped coroutines — interviews probe awareness.
Modules: the end of header hell (in theory). Know what they solve (compile times, macro leakage) and the adoption reality (tooling still catching up).
std::format, std::span, std::jthread, designated initializers: the everyday modern toolkit. Using printf-style or C arrays in new code signals stale knowledge.

example.walkthrough: 'Modern C++' in interviews means: do you write 2020s C++ or 1990s C++ with a new compiler? Concepts, ranges, and smart ownership are the shibboleths.

pitfalls: SFINAE where concepts fit — unreadable errors are a choice now, not a necessity.
Raw new/delete in new code — make_unique/make_shared exist; use them.
C-style casts and arrays — static_cast, std::array/span; the old forms are code smells.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite one old-style function you know (raw loop + C array) using ranges + span. Compare readability.

lessons.title: System Design for C++ Engineers
concepts: C++ system design interviews test: concurrency architecture, memory layout awareness, and latency thinking — not just 'which database'.
Lead with constraints: throughput? latency p99? memory budget? The numbers choose the architecture — 1M msg/sec needs lock-free queues; 1K/sec needs clarity.
Talk data flow: where does data live, who mutates it, how do threads coordinate? Draw the ownership and the synchronization — the diagram IS the answer.
Latency vocabulary: cache misses (~100ns), syscalls (~1µs), network (~100µs-1ms). Budget the p99 from these — interviewers love the arithmetic.
Trade-off close: 'I'd start with X for clarity; if profiling shows Y, I'd switch to Z.' Decisions with escape hatches beat premature optimization.

example.code:
Design: 100k msg/sec market data fan-out, p99 < 1ms.
  Ingest: lock-free SPSC queue per producer (no contention)
  Process: single-threaded matching (no locks, cache-hot)
  Fan-out: shared-memory ring to consumers
  p99 budget: queue (100ns) + process (10µs) + ring (1µs) — fits.
  The numbers justify every choice.
example.walkthrough: System design for C++ roles is latency arithmetic + concurrency architecture. Lead with numbers, draw the data flow, name the trade-offs.

pitfalls: No numbers — 'fast' is not a requirement; quantify or guess explicitly.
Locks everywhere — the default that kills p99; design lock-free first.
Ignoring the memory layout — cache behavior IS the performance story.
lessons.try_it: Design a 10k req/sec key-value cache on paper: data structures, threading, p99 budget. Time: 20 min.

lessons.title: Lock-Free Programming Basics
concepts: Lock-free = at least one thread always progresses (vs wait-free = all do). The goal is usually avoiding mutex contention in hot paths — not ideology.
The atomics toolkit: load/store, exchange, compare_exchange_weak/strong (CAS loop). CAS is the fundamental primitive — everything lock-free builds on it.
Memory ordering: seq_cst (safest, slowest), acquire/release (the workhorse pairing), relaxed (counters only, with proof). Default seq_cst until profiling + reasoning justify less.
ABA problem: CAS succeeds but the value changed A→B→A underneath. Solutions: tagged pointers, hazard pointers, epoch reclamation. Know it exists; use libraries for the hard parts.
Rule: use battle-tested lock-free structures (moodycamel queues, folly) before hand-rolling. Hand-rolled lock-free is where careers go to debug.

example.walkthrough: Lock-free is a scalpel for profiled contention, not a default. Understand CAS and ordering; use libraries for production; hand-roll only to learn.

pitfalls: Hand-rolled lock-free in production — subtle, untestable edge cases; use libraries.
Relaxed ordering without proof — the bugs are heisenbugs; default seq_cst.
Ignoring ABA — the classic lock-free trap; know it by name.
lessons.try_it: Implement the lock-free stack above. Then find one bug class it has (hint: ABA/memory reclamation).

lessons.title: Benchmarking Rigorously
concepts: Benchmark with Google Benchmark or equivalent: it handles warmup, repetition, and statistics. Hand-rolled timers lie (cold caches, single runs, noise).
Rules: warm up, many iterations, report median (not mean — outliers skew), disable CPU frequency scaling, pin to a core, close the browser. Rigor is the result.
Prevent optimization elision: benchmark::DoNotOptimize(result) — otherwise the compiler deletes your 'work' and you benchmark nothing.
Compare correctly: A/B on the same machine, same load, interleaved runs. 'My laptop vs the server' is not a benchmark — it is two anecdotes.
Statistical significance: if the error bars overlap, there is no winner. Report confidence intervals, not just means — honesty in numbers.

example.walkthrough: Bad benchmarks are worse than no benchmarks: they justify wrong decisions with numbers. Rigor is not pedantry — it is the difference between data and decoration.

pitfalls: Single-run timing — noise dominates; repeat and take medians.
No DoNotOptimize — the compiler optimized away your benchmark; you measured nothing.
Mean without variance — overlapping error bars mean no conclusion; report the spread.
lessons.try_it: Benchmark vector push_back vs reserve+push_back with Google Benchmark (or a careful manual harness). Report median + spread.

lessons.title: C++23: What's Actually Useful
concepts: std::expected: the error-handling upgrade — return expected<Value, Error> instead of exceptions or error codes. Explicit, composable, no overhead. The biggest practical C++23 feature.
Deducing this: explicit object parameters simplify CRTP and recursive lambdas. `void f(this auto&& self)` — cleaner forwarding, less boilerplate.
Ranges upgrades: more adaptors (zip, chunk, slide), ranges::to for container conversion. The ranges library keeps growing into the obvious gaps.
std::mdspan: non-owning multidimensional views — the scientific computing crowd's long wait is over. Think span, but N-dimensional.
Adoption reality: compiler support is rolling out; library features land first. Learn the concepts now, adopt per your toolchain's support — check, don't assume.

example.walkthrough: C++23's theme is 'explicit and composable': expected for errors, deducing-this for cleaner generics. Learn the ideas; adopt as toolchains allow.

pitfalls: Assuming full support — check your compiler version; C++23 is still rolling out.
Ignoring std::expected — it is the most broadly useful addition; learn it first.
Chasing every feature — concepts/ranges (C++20) matter more today than C++23 novelties.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite one error-code function using std::expected (or sketch it). Compare readability with the old version.

lessons.title: References vs Pointers: The Complete Picture
concepts: References are aliases: must be initialized, cannot be reseated, cannot be null. Use for in/out parameters and range-for. Pointers are addresses: can be null, reseated, do arithmetic.
Prefer references for parameters (caller syntax stays clean); pointers when null is meaningful or reseating is needed. const& for read-only large params — the default.
Dangling references: returning a reference to a local is UB. Lifetime extension applies to temporaries bound in the same scope — not across function returns.
Member init order: initialization list order follows DECLARATION order, not list order. Mismatches compile with warnings and confuse — match them.
auto&& and forwarding references: in templates, auto&& binds to anything and preserves value category. Know when you are forwarding vs copying.

example.walkthrough: Choose reference vs pointer by semantics: alias or address? The type should say what you mean — reviewers read types first.

pitfalls: Non-const reference for read-only params — blocks temporaries; use const&.
Returning references to locals — UB that often 'works'; the worst kind of bug.
Init-list order mismatch — subtle initialization bugs; match declaration order.
lessons.try_it: Audit one function you wrote: are its reference/pointer choices semantically right? Fix one.

lessons.title: const Correctness: A Discipline
concepts: const on methods: `int get() const` promises not to mutate. Callers with const objects can only call const methods — const-correctness is viral; start at the leaves.
const& parameters: no copy, no mutation. The default for in-parameters of class type. Pass by value only for small trivial types.
mutable for caches: logically-const but physically-mutating (memoization, mutexes). mutable is the escape hatch — use sparingly and document.
const_cast is a code smell: if you need it, the design is wrong somewhere. The rare legit uses (legacy APIs) deserve comments explaining why.
constexpr: compute at compile time when possible. constexpr functions are testable, fast (zero runtime cost), and increasingly capable.

example.walkthrough: const-correctness is a contract with your callers: 'I will not surprise you.' Apply it from day one — retrofitting is painful.

pitfalls: Non-const getters — blocks use in const contexts; the virality punishes late adoption.
const_cast to 'fix' const issues — the design is wrong; fix the design.
Missing constexpr opportunities — compile-time computation is free performance.
lessons.try_it: Add const to every method that qualifies in one of your classes. What breaks? Fix the call sites properly.

lessons.title: Virtual Dispatch: Costs and Rules
concepts: Virtual functions dispatch at runtime via vtable: one indirection per call. The cost is tiny per call but real in hot loops — know it, measure before avoiding.
Destructor MUST be virtual in polymorphic base classes: deleting via base pointer without virtual dtor is UB. This is the #1 OOP interview trap.
override specifier: marks intent, catches signature mismatches at compile time. Always use it — the compiler becomes your reviewer.
NVI (non-virtual interface): public non-virtual method calls private virtual implementation. Base controls the protocol (logging, locking); derived customizes the behavior.
Prefer composition over inheritance: inheritance is the tightest coupling in the language. 'Is-a' rarely; 'has-a' usually. Interfaces (pure virtual) for polymorphism.

example.walkthrough: Inheritance is for polymorphism, not code reuse. When you reach for inheritance, ask: 'do I need runtime polymorphism here?' If not, compose.

pitfalls: Non-virtual destructor in base — UB on polymorphic delete; the classic trap.
Missing override — silent non-override when signatures drift; always annotate.
Deep inheritance hierarchies — brittle, hard to reason about; prefer composition + interfaces.
lessons.try_it: Find an inheritance hierarchy you know. Could composition + interfaces replace it? Sketch the alternative.

lessons.title: CRTP and Policy-Based Design
concepts: CRTP (curiously recurring template pattern): class D : public Base<D>. Static polymorphism — no vtable, no runtime cost. The base customizes via the derived type.
Use CRTP for: static interfaces, mixins (counted objects, cloneable), and compile-time customization. It is inheritance for performance, not for runtime flexibility.
Policy-based design: template parameters ARE the policies (e.g., StoragePolicy, ThreadingModel). Compose behavior at compile time — Alexandrescu's Modern C++ Design pattern.
Trade-off: zero runtime cost, but binary bloat (each instantiation is new code) and harder debugging (template errors). Measure the binary size impact.
Modern alternative: concepts constrain the policies (C++20), making misuse readable. CRTP + concepts = static polymorphism with good errors.

example.walkthrough: CRTP is the power tool for 'I want polymorphism but cannot afford virtual': libraries, embedded, hot paths. Reach for it deliberately, not by default.

pitfalls: CRTP for runtime-flexible designs — static means static; if you need runtime plugin behavior, use virtual.
Ignoring binary bloat — 50 instantiations of a big CRTP base is 50 copies; measure.
Unconstrained templates — C++20 concepts turn novel-length errors into one line.
lessons.try_it: Implement a CRTP mixin (e.g., a cloneable or counted base). Instantiate for 2 types; verify no virtuals in the disassembly (or just trust the pattern).

lessons.title: Inheritance vs Composition in Practice
concepts: The test: 'is-a' must survive the Liskov substitution — a Square IS-A Rectangle fails (resizing breaks the contract). Most 'is-a' intuitions fail LSP; composition survives.
Composition benefits: looser coupling, runtime flexibility (swap components), easier testing (mock the parts). The composed object delegates; it does not inherit problems.
Inheritance costs: fragile base class (base changes break derived silently), namespace pollution, and the diamond (virtual inheritance as band-aid). Each has bitten real codebases.
Interface inheritance (pure virtual) is the safe kind: it specifies WHAT without dictating HOW. Abstract bases with no data members age gracefully.
Refactoring rule: when a hierarchy grows past 2-3 levels, flatten to composition + strategy objects. Depth is the smell; delegation is the fix.

example.walkthrough: Default to composition; use inheritance only for true interface polymorphism. Your future self maintains this code — choose the flexible structure.

pitfalls: Deep hierarchies for code reuse — reuse via composition; hierarchies are for polymorphism.
Concrete base classes with data — the fragile base class problem; keep bases abstract.
LSP violations — if substituting the derived breaks expectations, the inheritance is wrong.
lessons.try_it: Take a 3+-level hierarchy you know. Refactor it to composition on paper. What got simpler?

lessons.title: Choosing Containers: The Decision Tree
concepts: Default to vector: contiguous, cache-friendly, and fast for 95% of uses. The 'which container' question usually ends here — justify anything else.
vector vs deque: deque allows efficient front insertion and never invalidates on growth (chunked). vector invalidates on reallocation. Need stable references + front ops? deque.
Associative: map/set (ordered, O(log n)), unordered_map/set (hashed, O(1) avg). Ordered when you iterate in order; hashed when you just look up.
list/forward_list: almost never. The cache-hostile node-based design loses to vector even with insertions — measure before choosing list; you will be surprised.
The real question is access pattern: random access → vector; frequent lookup → unordered_map; ordered traversal → map; FIFO → queue/deque.

example.walkthrough: Container choice is a performance decision disguised as a style choice. Default vector; deviate with measurements, not feelings.

pitfalls: list by default ('lots of insertions') — vector usually wins anyway; benchmark first.
map when unordered_map suffices — paying O(log n) for order you never use.
Ignoring invalidation rules — vector reallocation invalidates; design lifetimes accordingly.
lessons.try_it: For your current project: list each container used and the access pattern justifying it. Any unjustified?

lessons.title: Iterators: The Glue of the STL
concepts: Iterator categories: input/output (single-pass), forward (multi-pass), bidirectional (+--), random-access (+[], arithmetic). Algorithms declare what they need; containers provide what they have.
Invalidation rules per container: vector (reallocation invalidates all), deque (insert invalidates all, erase only erased), list/map (only erased element). Know your container's rules cold.
Erase-remove idiom: v.erase(remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(), pred), v.end()). remove_if compacts; erase deletes. The two-step is the correct pattern — memorize it.
Range-based for is for reading; iterators are for mutating structure. Erasing while range-for-ing is UB — use the iterator loop with it = c.erase(it).
C++20 ranges: views are lazy and composable (filter | transform). Prefer ranges for expressiveness; fall back to iterators where mutation or performance demands.

example.walkthrough: Iterators are the STL's abstraction for 'position'. Master invalidation rules and the erase-remove idiom — they prevent the most common container bugs.

pitfalls: Erasing in range-for — UB; use iterator loop with erase's return.
Using removed elements — remove_if doesn't erase; the tail is garbage until erase.
Assuming iterator stability — check invalidation rules per operation, per container.
lessons.try_it: Write the erase-remove idiom from memory. Then write the iterator-loop erase version. Both must compile mentally.

lessons.title: Associative Containers Deep Dive
concepts: unordered_map internals: bucket array + hash function. Load factor triggers rehash (invalidates iterators). Reserve bucket count upfront when size is known.
Hash quality matters: std::hash is fine for ints/strings; custom types need custom hashes combining member hashes (hash_combine pattern). Bad hashes = O(n) buckets.
map (tree) guarantees: ordered iteration, O(log n) ops, no rehash invalidation. Use when order matters or worst-case guarantees beat average-case speed.
Heterogeneous lookup (C++20): map<string,...>.find("literal") without constructing std::string — transparent comparators (std::less<>) avoid temporaries.
Flat alternatives: absl::flat_hash_map / robin_hood hashing (open addressing) beat std::unordered_map on cache behavior. Know they exist for hot paths.

example.walkthrough: Hash containers are engineered structures: buckets, load factors, hash quality. The defaults work; the tuning wins when profiles say so.

pitfalls: Default-constructed unordered_map for 1M inserts — rehash storms; reserve upfront.
Bad custom hash (e.g., return 0) — degenerate O(n) buckets; test hash distribution.
map for pure lookup workloads — paying for order never used; profile first.
lessons.try_it: Benchmark: 100k inserts+lookups, map vs unordered_map (reserved) vs unordered_map (default). Report the ratios.

lessons.title: unique_ptr Patterns
concepts: make_unique is the only way to create: no bare new, exception-safe, single allocation intent. `auto p = std::make_unique<Widget>(args)` — always.
Transferring ownership: std::move into functions (sink), return by value (source). The type system tracks ownership — moved-from is empty, provably.
unique_ptr in containers: vector<unique_ptr<Widget>> owns polymorphic objects. Move-only elements work fine with emplace_back(std::make_unique...).
Custom deleters: unique_ptr<FILE, decltype(&fclose)> for C resources. RAII for everything — files, handles, locks. No raw resource should outlive its scope.
Pimpl idiom: unique_ptr<Impl> in header, defined in .cpp. Compilation firewall — change impl without recompiling dependents. The professional's encapsulation.

example.walkthrough: unique_ptr makes ownership visible and transfer explicit. If your code's ownership is unclear, the types are wrong — fix the types.

pitfalls: Bare new assigned to unique_ptr — exception-unsafe between new and construction; use make_unique.
unique_ptr for shared ownership — that is shared_ptr's job; pick by semantics.
Forgetting move on transfer — copy of unique_ptr doesn't compile; the error is the teacher.
lessons.try_it: Convert one raw-new/delete pair in your code to make_unique. Verify no leaks with ASan.

lessons.title: shared_ptr: Costs and Cycles
concepts: shared_ptr costs: control block allocation (unless make_shared), atomic refcount increments (thread-safe but not free), and indirection. Measure before using in hot paths.
make_shared: single allocation for object + control block. Faster, exception-safe, one allocation — always prefer it. (Slight caveat: memory held until all weak_ptrs die.)
Cycles kill: A↔B shared_ptrs never reach zero. Break with weak_ptr on the back-reference (parent→child shared, child→parent weak). Draw the ownership graph; find the cycle.
weak_ptr usage: lock() to temporary shared_ptr, check validity. Observers, caches, and back-pointers — the non-owning roles.
Aliasing constructor: shared_ptr<Widget> shares ownership with shared_ptr<Container> but points at the member. Advanced — know it exists for lifetime extension patterns.

example.walkthrough: shared_ptr is for genuinely shared ownership — rarer than people think. Default unique_ptr; promote to shared only when sharing is real, and break cycles with weak_ptr.

pitfalls: shared_ptr by default — atomic refcounts in hot loops; unique_ptr is free.
Cycles (parent↔child both shared) — the silent leak; weak_ptr breaks it.
make_shared caveat ignored — weak_ptrs keep the whole allocation alive; know the trade.
lessons.try_it: Draw the ownership graph of a structure you own. Any cycles? Fix one with weak_ptr.

lessons.title: Custom Allocators and Memory Pools
concepts: Default allocator does heap per allocation: fine generally, slow for many small objects (fragmentation, syscall overhead). Pools allocate chunks and subdivide — O(1) amortized.
pmr (C++17): std::pmr::vector<T> with memory_resource — monotonic_buffer_resource for phase-based allocation (parse everything, release at once). Zero per-object overhead.
Pool pattern: fixed-size blocks, free list. Game engines, network servers (per-connection buffers), parsers — anywhere allocation rate is high and sizes are uniform.
Alignment matters: over-aligned types (SIMD) need aligned allocation. alignas + aligned new — or the allocator must guarantee it. UB otherwise.
Measure first: heaptrack/malloc_stats show allocation hotspots. Optimize the allocator only when allocation IS the profiled bottleneck — it usually isn't.

example.walkthrough: Custom allocation is a scalpel for profiled hotspots, not a default. The default allocator is good; pmr/pools are for measured pain.

pitfalls: Premature pool-ification — complexity without a profiled need.
Pool without alignment care — SIMD types crash or slow on misaligned pool memory.
Forgetting pmr propagation — nested containers need the resource passed down; defaults silently heap-allocate.
lessons.try_it: Profile allocations in a program you have (heaptrack or even counting new calls). Is allocation actually hot?

lessons.title: Function Templates: The Basics Done Right
concepts: Type deduction: template args deduced from function args (no need to specify). Deduction rules mirror auto — references collapse, arrays decay unless taken by reference.
Put templates in headers (or modules): the compiler needs the definition at instantiation. The linker error for missing definitions is the classic template headache.
Non-type params and auto params (C++20): template<auto N> works for values. Concepts constrain: template<std::integral T> — readable errors instead of novel-length spew.
Overload resolution with templates: non-template preferred if equally good; then most specialized. Understand the ranking or overload sets surprise you.
Explicit instantiation: template class Foo<int>; in a .cpp — compiles once, links everywhere. For library authors hiding implementation (with known type sets).

example.walkthrough: Templates are compile-time duck typing with (now) readable constraints. Concepts turned the error messages from punishment into guidance — use them.

pitfalls: Definitions in .cpp without explicit instantiation — linker errors; templates live in headers.
Unconstrained templates — C++20 concepts exist; SFINAE is legacy.
Over-specifying template args — let deduction work; specify only when it cannot.
lessons.try_it: Write a constrained function template (concept) you would actually use. Trigger the error deliberately — admire its readability.

lessons.title: Variadic Templates and Fold Expressions
concepts: Parameter packs: template<typename... Ts> captures any number of types. sizeof...(Ts) counts them. The pack must be expanded to be useful.
Fold expressions (C++17): (args + ...) folds with +. Unary folds need the pattern obvious: (std::cout << ... << args) prints all. Folds replaced pages of recursion.
Perfect forwarding: template<typename... A> f(A&&... a) { g(std::forward<A>(a)...); } — preserves value categories through the forwarding chain. The && here is forwarding, not rvalue.
Use cases: type-safe printf, tuple implementation, factory functions, visitor patterns. Variadics shine where arity varies — factories and emplace.
Compile-time cost: deep recursion in old-style variadics slowed builds; folds are cheap. Prefer folds; reserve recursion for genuinely recursive structures.

example.walkthrough: Folds made variadics humane: one line where recursion needed twenty. Reach for folds first; recursion only for tree-shaped problems.

pitfalls: Recursive variadics where folds suffice — 10x the code, 10x the compile time.
Forgetting std::forward in forwarding — copies where moves were intended; the && is half the story.
Pack expansion in the wrong place — the ... position matters; misplaced packs are cryptic errors.
lessons.try_it: Write print_all above from memory. Then extend it with a separator using a fold with a helper lambda.

lessons.title: Lambdas: Captures and Gotchas
concepts: Capture list is the contract: [=] copies, [&] references, [x] specific copy, [&x] specific ref, [this] member access. Default captures ([=]/[&]) are convenient and dangerous — prefer explicit.
Dangling captures: [&] lambda outliving the scope — the async callback capturing locals by reference. #1 lambda bug. Capture by value (or shared_ptr) for anything escaping.
mutable lambdas: [=] captures are const by default; mutable allows mutation of the COPIES. Rarely needed — usually a sign to restructure.
Generic lambdas: auto params (C++14) make lambdas templates. [](auto x){ return x*2; } — perfect for STL algorithms and callbacks.
std::function overhead: type erasure costs (virtual call + maybe allocation). Hot paths: templates/auto params instead. std::function is for type-erased storage, not speed.

example.walkthrough: The capture list deserves the same care as a function signature: it defines lifetime and ownership. Review every capture for 'will this outlive its source?'

pitfalls: [&] on escaping lambdas — the dangling capture; the most common lambda UB.
Default captures hiding lifetime bugs — explicit captures force the lifetime question.
std::function in hot loops — type-erasure overhead; templates are free.
lessons.try_it: Find a lambda you wrote with [&]. Does it escape its scope? Convert to explicit captures and verify safety.

lessons.title: CMake: The 20% That Covers 80%
concepts: Modern CMake (3.14+): target-based (target_link_libraries, target_include_directories), not directory-based. Targets carry their usage requirements — transitive correctness for free.
The minimal modern CMakeLists: cmake_minimum_required, project, add_library/add_executable, target_link_libraries with PUBLIC/PRIVATE. Five commands cover most projects.
PUBLIC vs PRIVATE: PUBLIC propagates to dependents (headers they need), PRIVATE stays internal. Getting this right makes downstream linking just work.
FetchContent for dependencies: FetchContent_Declare + MakeAvailable downloads at configure time. Vendoring without submodules — reproducible builds.
Out-of-source builds always: cmake -B build && cmake --build build. Never pollute the source tree — the build dir is disposable.

example.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(myapp)
add_library(core src/a.cpp src/b.cpp)
target_include_directories(core PUBLIC include)
target_link_libraries(core PRIVATE fmt::fmt)
add_executable(app src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE core)
example.walkthrough: Modern CMake is declarative dependency management: describe targets and their relationships; the tool handles the graph. Learn the target model once.

pitfalls: Directory-based commands (include_directories) — global pollution; use target_* versions.
In-source builds — pollutes the repo; always -B build.
Missing PUBLIC/PRIVATE — dependents fail to link; the keywords exist for a reason.
lessons.try_it: Convert any old CMakeLists you have to target-based. Verify the build still works.

lessons.title: Sanitizers: Your Automated Reviewers
concepts: ASan (address): use-after-free, heap overflow, double-free — the memory bugs. -fsanitize=address. 2x slowdown, enormous bug-finding value.
TSan (thread): data races — the concurrency bugs. -fsanitize=thread. Needs all code (including libs) built with TSan for full accuracy.
UBSan (undefined behavior): signed overflow, null deref, misaligned access — the 'works by accident' bugs. -fsanitize=undefined. Cheapest to run.
Workflow: debug build + sanitizers on every test run. CI runs the sanitizer suite; clean sanitizer output is a merge requirement.
They find bugs testing misses: sanitizers catch the UB that 'works' in tests but breaks in production. Run them always in dev/test.

example.code:
# CMake sanitizer preset:
set(SAN_FLAGS "-fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer")
set(CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG "${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG} ${SAN_FLAGS}")
set(CMAKE_LINKER_FLAGS_DEBUG "${CMAKE_LINKER_FLAGS_DEBUG} ${SAN_FLAGS}")
# Every test run now hunts memory bugs automatically.
example.walkthrough: Sanitizers are the highest-ROI testing investment in C++: they find entire bug CLASSES automatically. Enable them before writing another test.

pitfalls: No sanitizers in CI — memory bugs ship to production; the 2x slowdown is nothing vs a CVE.
TSan on partial builds — mixed instrumentation gives false confidence; build all with TSan.
Ignoring UBSan reports — 'works fine' UB is still UB; the optimizer will exploit it eventually.
lessons.try_it: Enable ASan+UBSan on your project's debug build. Run the tests. Triage the first report.

lessons.title: Debugging With GDB Like a Pro
concepts: Build with -g -O0 for debugging: full symbols, no optimization surprises. Debug the build you ship? Use -g -O2 and accept some variable weirdness.
Breakpoints with conditions: break foo.cpp:42 if x > 100 — stop only when interesting. Watchpoints: watch var stops on write. These beat printf debugging.
Backtrace literacy: bt shows the call stack; frame N + info locals inspects. 'Where am I and how did I get here' answers 50% of bugs.
TUI mode (gdb -tui or Ctrl-X A): source + assembly + prompt. Seeing the code while stepping transforms debugging speed.
Core dumps: ulimit -c unlimited, then gdb ./app core. Post-mortem debugging — the crash already happened; the core has the answers.

example.code:
Crashing program:
  $ ulimit -c unlimited && ./app   # segfault, core dumped
  $ gdb ./app core
  (gdb) bt          # the crash stack — frame 0 is the crime scene
  (gdb) frame 0
  (gdb) info locals # the values that killed it
  Five commands from mystery to root cause.
example.walkthrough: Learn the debugger before you need it at 2 AM: breakpoints, watchpoints, backtraces, cores. printf debugging does not scale to real bugs.

pitfalls: Debugging -O2 builds first — optimized-out variables confuse; start -O0.
No core dumps configured — the crash evidence vanishes; ulimit -c unlimited.
printf-only debugging — works for logic errors, fails for memory corruption; use the tools.
lessons.try_it: Generate a core from a crashing test program. Debug it with bt + info locals. Time yourself.

lessons.title: Talking Through Code Reviews
concepts: Review the code, not the coder: phrase every finding as an observation about the code ('this loop is O(n^2)') plus its consequence ('at 50k entries that's 2.5B comparisons'), never as a judgment of the author.
Separate blocking from nitpicking: correctness, UB, lifetime, and concurrency issues block; style preferences get labeled 'nit' and never hold up a merge.
Always propose the fix shape, not just the problem: 'use string_view here to avoid the copy' teaches; 'this copies' just criticizes.
In interviews, narrate your review out loud in priority order — interviewers score whether you find the dangling reference before you comment on brace style.

example.walkthrough: This comment names the mechanism (dangling view), the trigger (caller's string lifetime), and two concrete fixes with their trade-offs. That's the bar: mechanism + consequence + fix, in three lines.

pitfalls: Pitfall: leading with style nits — it signals you missed the lifetime bug on line 12 while bikeshedding line 3.
Pitfall: 'LGTM' on code with UB — approving a data race makes it your incident too.
Pitfall: rewriting the author's code in review — suggest the shape, let them own the implementation.
lessons.try_it: Take any 100-line C++ file, review it aloud in 10 minutes with findings ranked blocking/nit, and check you caught lifetime and concurrency issues before style.

lessons.title: Estimating Algorithm Costs Live
concepts: Fermi-estimate in layers: payload bytes, then per-entry overhead (allocations, pointers, padding), then container overhead (buckets, nodes) — overhead usually dominates, often 2-3x the payload.
Know the canonical sizes: pointer 8B, std::string 32B (SSO), unordered_map node ~32B+ overhead, cache line 64B, page 4KB — these are your estimating atoms.
Time estimates work the same way: operations per second per core (~3B simple ops), memory bandwidth (~20GB/s), network RTT — then divide the workload by the bottleneck resource.
State assumptions out loud and refine: 'assuming 20-char keys and SSO disabled...' — interviewers grade the reasoning chain, not the final number.

example.walkthrough: The estimate decomposes into named components so the interviewer can follow and correct any atom. The lever falls out naturally: the overhead components (node, string alloc) are exactly what a flat container eliminates.

pitfalls: Pitfall: multiplying payload only — you'll be 2-3x low and miss the actual design insight.
Pitfall: false precision — '8.53GB' from guessed inputs is theater; '8-10GB' with named assumptions is engineering.
Pitfall: freezing on the number — the estimate is a means to the lever, not the deliverable.
lessons.try_it: Estimate the memory of 10M ints in vector vs list vs unordered_set on paper, then verify with a 20-line program using mallinfo or a custom counter — calibrate your atoms.

lessons.title: Mutex vs Atomic Decision Guide
concepts: Atomics are for single locations: counters, flags, and simple state machines on trivially-copyable types — one indivisible operation on one word.
Mutexes are for invariants across locations: 'transfer money' touches two balances that must change together — no atomic spans two words.

Cost shape differs: uncontended atomics are ~tens of cycles and lock-free; uncontended mutexes are similar, but contended mutexes sleep (good for long waits) while contended atomics spin (good for short waits).
volatile is not synchronization: it stops some compiler optimizations but provides no atomicity, no ordering, and no visibility guarantees — it has no place in threading decisions.

example.walkthrough: The counter is one location: atomic, relaxed ordering since only the count matters. The transfer is a two-location invariant: only a mutex makes both updates indivisible to observers. The decision rule is structural, not stylistic.

pitfalls: Pitfall: atomic for multi-location invariants — two atomics don't compose into one atomic transaction.
Pitfall: mutex around a hot flag poll — serializes 32 threads to protect one byte; atomic<bool> exists for this.
Pitfall: reaching for volatile — it compiles, it runs, and it races.
lessons.try_it: Audit three shared variables in a codebase you know: classify each as single-location or multi-location invariant, and check the primitive matches — convert any mismatches.

lessons.title: Deadlock-Free Lock Ordering
concepts: Deadlock needs four conditions (Coffman): mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait — break any one and deadlock is impossible; lock ordering breaks circular wait.
The rule: define a global order (by address, by layer, by documented rank) and always acquire in that order — two threads acquiring A-then-B can never deadlock with each other.
std::lock and std::scoped_lock acquire multiple mutexes atomically without deadlock — use them when the order isn't statically knowable.
Keep critical sections small and never call unknown code (callbacks, virtuals) while holding a lock — it hides lock acquisitions that violate your ordering.

example.walkthrough: scoped_lock internally uses std::lock's deadlock-avoidance algorithm, so even if a future path wants the locks in a different conceptual order, acquisition is safe. The documented global order (accounts before audit) is the human-readable backup.

pitfalls: Pitfall: 'we'll be careful' instead of an enforced order — the AB-BA inversion always arrives via the new code path nobody reviewed for locking.
Pitfall: locking in destructors or callbacks — the hidden acquisition site that breaks the documented order.
Pitfall: try_lock retry loops without backoff — converts deadlock into livelock under contention.
lessons.try_it: Map every mutex in one subsystem, draw the acquisition graph across all code paths, and find any cycle — then fix it with a documented order or scoped_lock.

lessons.title: Reading a Profiler Flame Graph
concepts: Width is cost: a frame's horizontal width is its share of samples (CPU time) — wide plateaus are where the program lives; narrow towers are details.
Read top-down for the call chain and scan for width: the widest frame you can eliminate or shrink is the optimization target, not the most interesting-looking tower.
Eliminate before optimizing: caching a result, skipping redundant work, or choosing a better algorithm beats micro-tuning the wide frame every time.
Sample, don't guess: profiles must come from production-like workloads — optimizing a benchmark's hot path that never fires in production is negative work.

example.code:
$ perf record -F 99 -g ./service   # sample with call graphs
$ perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > out.svg
# Read: widest plateau = first target. Ask 'can this run less
# often?' before 'can this run faster?'
example.walkthrough: The workflow is mechanical: capture under realistic load, render, find the widest plateau, and interrogate necessity before speed. Most flame-graph wins come from deleting calls, not accelerating them.

pitfalls: Pitfall: optimizing the narrow tower because it's 'clearly inefficient' — 2% of samples optimized 10x is 0.2% total.
Pitfall: profiling debug builds — inlining and optimization change the shape completely; always profile optimized binaries with symbols.
Pitfall: one profile, permanent conclusions — workloads drift; re-profile after every significant change.
lessons.try_it: Profile any program you own for 60 seconds under realistic load, render the flame graph, and write down the top-3 widest frames with a 'can it run less often?' answer for each.

lessons.title: Cache-Friendly Data Layout
concepts: CPUs move 64-byte cache lines, not bytes: touching one byte pulls 64, so sequential access gets 16 floats per miss while strided access pays a miss per element.
Structure-of-arrays beats array-of-structures for hot loops: iterating positions over 1M particles streams 4MB contiguously in SoA, versus striding over 64-byte structs touching 64MB in AoS.
Match traversal to layout: row-major storage demands row-inner loops; if the algorithm needs column access, transpose the data once instead of paying strided access forever.
False sharing is the coherence tax: keep independently-written fields on separate cache lines (alignas(64)) or watch cores serialize on the interconnect.

example.walkthrough: The transform is mechanical: identify the hot field subset, split it into its own contiguous arrays, and watch the miss rate collapse. The win comes from the memory system, not the ALU — the math didn't change at all.

pitfalls: Pitfall: optimizing the ALU while the memory system starves — a 2x faster inner loop on cache-missing data gains nothing.
Pitfall: SoA everywhere — it complicates code; apply it to the hot loops the profiler names, not the whole codebase.
Pitfall: ignoring prefetch-friendliness — even SoA loses if the access pattern jumps randomly; sort or reorder for sequential access.
lessons.try_it: Take a loop over an array-of-structs, measure its cache-miss rate with perf stat, convert to SoA, and measure again — record the miss-rate and wall-time deltas.

lessons.title: Move Semantics in Practice
concepts: Move = steal the guts: a move constructor transfers the heap buffer pointer instead of copying 10MB, leaving the source in a valid-but-unspecified state — O(1) instead of O(n).
Return by value freely: C++17 guaranteed elision plus move fallback means `return big_vector;` never copies — out-parameters for 'performance' are obsolete pessimization.
std::move is a cast, not an action: it marks an lvalue as movable; the move constructor does the work — and moving from an object you still use is a bug.
Rule of five interaction: declaring a move constructor suppresses the copy operations — if your type should copy, declare or default them explicitly.

example.walkthrough: The return transfers ownership of the buffer: either the compiler constructs directly into the caller's vector (elision) or the move constructor steals the pointer. Either way the 10MB is never duplicated — the code reads naturally and performs optimally.

pitfalls: Pitfall: `return std::move(out);` — inhibits NRVO and forces a move where elision would have been free.
Pitfall: moving from const objects — binds to the copy constructor instead, silently copying.
Pitfall: using a moved-from object beyond destruction/assignment — valid but unspecified state is not 'empty and safe to read'.
lessons.try_it: Write a type with noisy copy/move constructors, return it from a function four ways (plain return, std::move return, out-param, const return), and log which operations actually run under -O2.

lessons.title: constexpr and consteval in Practice
concepts: constexpr shifts pure computation to compile time: lookup tables, hash constants, and parser tables get baked into the binary with zero startup cost.
consteval (C++20) is stricter: the function MUST run at compile time — use it when runtime execution would be a bug (e.g., compile-time-validated format strings).
constexpr functions can still run at runtime when given runtime arguments — the same code serves both worlds, which is why standard algorithms are increasingly constexpr.
constinit guarantees static initialization (no static-init-order fiasco) without requiring full constness — the right tool for globals that must be ready before main().

example.walkthrough: The immediately-invoked lambda builds the table in a constexpr context, so the compiler emits 256 constants into .rodata — every process startup and every test binary skips the computation entirely, and the values stay derived from the algorithm.

pitfalls: Pitfall: assuming constexpr means compile-time — it means compile-time-capable; verify with static_assert or constinit where it matters.
Pitfall: constexpr with hidden runtime dependencies (RNG, I/O, virtual calls) — fails to constant-evaluate, sometimes silently falling back to runtime.
Pitfall: over-constexpring huge computations — multi-second compile-time table builds tax every developer's build; keep them proportional.
lessons.try_it: Convert one startup-computed lookup table in a project to constexpr, add a static_assert on two entries, and compare binary startup time before/after.

lessons.title: const Correctness from Day One
concepts: const is a compile-time contract: `const` on a method promises no mutation, `const` on a reference promises no mutation through that reference — the compiler enforces both.
Read declarations right-to-left: `const std::string&` is a reference to a const string; `std::string* const` is a const pointer to a mutable string — precision here prevents real bugs.
const-correctness is viral and that's good: one const object requires const accessors, which require const-correct callees — the chain pushes correctness through the whole design.
Retrofitting const is painful; starting const is free: default to const references for in-parameters and const methods for accessors, and remove const only with a reason.

example.walkthrough: The accessor is callable on const Config objects and returns without copying; the setter takes a const reference so callers pass temporaries safely. Every const here was a one-word decision that the compiler now enforces forever.

pitfalls: Pitfall: 'discards qualifiers' errors — they mean a const object met a non-const method; fix the method, not the caller's constness.
Pitfall: const_cast to 'fix' compilation — lies to the compiler; mutating a genuinely-const object is undefined behavior.
Pitfall: returning const values from functions — blocks move semantics for no benefit in modern C++.
lessons.try_it: Take one class you wrote, make every accessor const and every in-parameter a const reference, and fix each compiler error by adding const (not removing it) — count how many latent mutation risks surface.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Container
concepts: Default to std::vector: contiguous storage gives the best iteration speed, cache behavior, and memory density — most programs' access pattern is 'iterate everything'.

Reach for node-based containers (list, map) only for iterator stability across insertions or true O(1) middle insertion with existing iterators — and measure, because cache misses often erase the theoretical win.
unordered_* trades ordering for average O(1) lookup but pays node overhead and hash cost; for small sizes (<~100 elements) a sorted vector with binary search often wins outright.

Know the invalidation rules cold: vector invalidates on reallocation (fix with reserve), deque invalidates on ends-insertion, node containers never invalidate on insert — pick by what your iterators must survive.

example.walkthrough: The flowchart starts from the access pattern, not the data: iteration favors contiguity, lookup favors hashing (at scale), stability favors nodes. Running any new container choice through these five questions takes ten seconds and prevents most container mistakes.

pitfalls: Pitfall: std::list by default 'because insertion is O(1)' — iteration-bound code runs 3-10x slower from pointer chasing.
Pitfall: std::map for everything keyed — unordered_map is usually faster for pure lookup; map only when ordering matters.
Pitfall: ignoring reserve() — a vector that reallocates 20 times during fill pays for the container choice twice.
lessons.try_it: Benchmark inserting 1M ints and then iterating them in vector vs list vs deque on your machine — record the wall times and explain the ratios from cache behavior.

simulations.title: Use after move
simulations.brief: A program crashes intermittently after a unique_ptr is passed to a worker function. The pointer looks valid at the call site.

steps.symptom: Intermittent crash inside process() — sometimes fine, sometimes SIGSEGV.
options: Read the ownership transfer: std::move gives the pointer away, so data is null afterward — the if (data) check can't save the logic error
Add a null check — the crash means the check is missing
The heap is corrupted; run with more memory
make_unique is buggy; use new instead
steps.explain: std::move transfers ownership: after the move, data is empty by design. The crash site is line 9's assumption that data still owns the buffer.

steps.symptom: Confirmed: data is empty after the move; line 9's use is logically dead.
options: Decide the intended ownership: if the caller still needs the buffer, pass by reference instead of moving
Keep the move and delete line 9
steps.explain: unique_ptr can't be copied — that's the point. If two parties need the buffer, pass a reference (or shared_ptr); if ownership truly transfers, remove the use-after-move.

steps.symptom: Fix chosen: pass by const reference. Verify the fix is complete.
options: Confirm worker takes const Buffer& and no std::move remains at the call site
Confirm data is still a unique_ptr
steps.explain: The fix is complete only when the signature borrows (const Buffer&) and the call site no longer moves — ownership never left the caller.

simulations.debrief: std::move is an ownership transfer, not a copy. After a move the source is empty by contract — audit every later use, or better, borrow with a reference when ownership shouldn't move.

simulations.title: The template error novel
simulations.brief: A template misuse produced 200 lines of diagnostics. Decide how to read them.

steps.text: The error output is 200 lines long, starting deep inside <vector> internals. Where do you look FIRST?

choices.label: The FIRST error — later errors are usually cascades from the first failure
choices.feedback: Correct: template errors cascade. The first diagnostic names the real constraint violation.

choices.label: The LAST error — it's the summary
choices.feedback: The last error is the deepest cascade, farthest from your code.

choices.label: The middle — it mentions your type name
choices.feedback: Tempting, but the middle is still cascade. Start at the top.

steps.text: The first error says: no matching function for call to 'push_back(int)' — the vector holds std::string. What's the fix?

choices.label: Push a std::string (or convert the int) — the container's element type is the contract
choices.feedback: Right: the template was instantiated correctly; the call site violated its contract.

choices.label: Change the vector to vector<int>
choices.feedback: Compiles, but it changes the program's meaning to silence the compiler.

choices.label: Add a cast at every push_back call site
choices.feedback: Casts at every call site hide the type error instead of fixing the contract.

simulations.debrief: Template diagnostics are novels: read the first error, ignore the cascade, and fix the contract violation at your call site — not the library's internals.

items: Most vexing parse — C++ grammar prefers to parse Widget w(); as a function declaration (returning Widget, taking no parameters) rather than a variable definition.

Uniform initialization — list initialization (braces) makes narrowing conversions — those that can lose information, like double→int — ill-formed. Brace initialization Widget w{} unambiguously defines an object — and additionally forbids narrowing conversions.

Common trap — the first declared overload always wins ties.

A using-directive in a header is transitive — everyone who includes it (directly or indirectly) gets the entire namespace injected, inviting collisions like a local count vs std::count and silently changing overload resolution. Keep using-directives in .cpp files after all includes, or qualify with std::.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For Core Syntax: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one OOP in C++ lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key STL Containers terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
